He said the restocking programme had given affected households an opportunity to rebuild their lives and regain economic independence. Former Igembe North Member of Parliament and Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service (KEPHIS) Board Chairman Joseph M’Eruaki welcomed the initiative but called for fairness, transparency and accountability throughout the distribution process. Speaking earlier during a church service at Athiru Catholic Church, M’Eruaki said only registered victims of cattle rustling should benefit from the programme and cautioned against favouritism or political interference. He also urged beneficiaries not to sell the livestock, saying the government’s objective is to rebuild herds, support dairy farming and restore sustainable livelihoods across the region. By Kamanja Maeria

Government to spend Sh10 million to desilt Kosowe Earth dam. The National Government through National Drought Management Autbority (NDMA) will spend Sh10 million to desilt Kosowe Earth Dam in Nzaui Subcounty with a view to increase its water capacity to 30,000 cubic meters, Makueni County Drought Co-ordinator (CDC) Alice Munyao has disclosed. Munyao made the disclosure in a County Steering Group meeting held at the County Commissioner’s Boardroom on Friday where she said that the desilting of the dam will take only three months to complete by October when the short rains are anticipated. The County Coordinator also revealed that the dam will benefit over 3,000 households with a view to end their perennial shortage of water in the area. “The works to desilt the Kisowe Earth Dam started on 16th July, and expect to be completed by early October before the short rain season commences,” Munyao said in the meeting that was chaired by the Deputy County Commissioner (DCC) who is also Personal Assistant in the County Commissioner’s office Peter Kimani on Friday. However, she never gave the name of the contractor undertaking the works at the dam. Also, she revealed her organization will spend another Sh3 million to purchase 300 Gala Goat that is aimed at improving the breed under the project and benefit 32 Nzakika Community groups. While saying goats are being procured currently, Munyao said that through the project, seeks to improve low goat productivity and household resilience in the Arid and Semi -Arid (ASAL) area hence help address poor genetics, inbreeding and climate stress with a view to improve the breed. She further said that the intervention is also expected to enhance growth rates, milk production and market value while maintaining adaptability to the harsh conditions in the area. The project is being implemented through the Wee Community Based Organization (CBO) in collaboration with NDMA and County Livestock Services at the county government. “The expected results include higher household incomes, improved nutrition and food security, better herd performance and strengthen community resilience, with sustainability ensured through revolving breeding schemes, skills transfer and strong institutional and community ownership,” she said. During the meeting the members were taken through the performance of the last rains of March, April and May that came earlier and was fairly distributed but farmers experienced reduced production because the reduction of rains that impacted on the crops. A Technical Committee was constituted comprising of the departments of Water, Health, Education, Agriculture, Livestock and NDMA to go and evaluate the impact of seasonal rains and other shocks on food and nutrition security and bring a report to be deliberated by the County Steering group on 24/07/2026. By Patrick Nyakundi

Ahero automated rice mill revolutionizes farmers’ incomes through value addition. Data from the Ministry of Agriculture shows Kenya imports about 740,000 to 900,000 metric tonnes of rice annually to meet its growing demand. The country consumes over one million metric tonnes each year, but local farms only produce about 150,000 to 230,000 metric tonnes which is just 14 per cent to 20 per cent of the nation’s ne forcing Kenya to heavily rely on imports (largely from Pakistan, India, and Tanzania) Kenya Kwanza`s Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA) aims to boost local rice production, cut heavy import costs, and ensure food security. The strategy is shifting from rain-fed farming to irrigation by rehabilitating 78,341 acres of existing schemes and opening 27,500 new acres to double output of rice in Kenya. For decades, Kano plains in Kisumu which is prone to flooding chocked under a punishing economic paradox; while the waters of the River Nyando provided the perfect conditions for intensive rice cultivation, the local farming community remained locked in a cycle of poverty. They did not have a choice but to sell their rice paddy at a throwaway price to middlemen because they did not have proper machines to mill it. Farmers sweated for months under a scorching sun only to hand their raw paddy over to outdated, erratic village hulling machines that crushed, fractured, and contaminated the grain, thus aggravating their agony and many times ended giving it to middlemen who went to mill it in Uganda. However, a towering industrial landmark has changed the whole story and now they are smiling all the way to the bank! Courtesy of the county government of Kisumu. The newly commissioned, Sh30 million automated Ahero Rice Mill has brought a high-tech mechanical revolution to the region, acting as the primary engine driving smallholder farming into a highly lucrative, modern commercial industry. Before the introduction of this multi-million shilling facility, the journey from harvest to market was a financial nightmare. Traditional milling methods across the plains relied on basic, single-pass machinery that lacked the capability to clean, de-stone, or properly polish the grain. This structural inefficiency meant that up to thirty percent of a farmer’s total harvest value was completely lost due to poor post-harvest handling and broken kernels. Unable to compete with clean, cheaply imported rice filling the supermarket shelves in Kisumu City, local farmers were forced to sell their sub-standard yields to exploitative middlemen at throwaway prices just to clear their debts. Thus, the installation of the automated factory has systematically dismantled this exploitative system by placing state-of-the-art value addition directly at the source. The Ahero Rice Mill is not just a standard hurler, it is a multi-stage, high-capacity industrial processing plant designed to clean, de-stone, hull, polish, and grade rice in a single, continuous, fully automated process. When raw paddy enters the facility, it undergoes a rigorous, mechanized purification process that separates dust, straws, and small rocks that manually operated sorting lines routinely miss. The process moves seamlessly from raw paddy input, through automated des-stoning and cleaning, careful hurling, followed by polishing and grading, before finishing at premium market packaging. By removing these impurities, the mill ensures that the local grain meets the highest national and international food quality standards. Furthermore, the high-volume daily processing capacity solves the massive regional crisis of post-harvest rot. During peak harvest seasons, a delayed milling schedule used to cause moisture accumulation within damp storage bags, leading to rapid fungal growth. With the new mill running consistently, thousands of tons of paddy are dried, hurled and safely packaged within minutes of arriving from the fields, stabilizing the local food supply chain and preserving grain integrity. For 54-year-old veteran farmer Tobias Omondi, the mechanical precision of the centralized mill has completely rescued his household from seasonal debt. ”In the past, taking my paddy to the local village mills felt like watching my money get ground into dust,” Omondi explains, standing outside the modern facility’s intake bay. “The old machines would crush the rice into small, broken pieces. If your rice is full of broken grains and tiny stones, no premium buyer will look at it. You are forced to sell it for nothing.” The narrative changed completely when Omondi began routing his seasonal harvest straight to the automated Ahero Rice Mill. ”The automated sorters handle the grain so gently that the percentage of broken rice has dropped to almost zero,” Omondi says. “I am getting clean, whole, premium-grade white rice that commands top shilling in city markets”. He says last season, because of the mill’s high efficiency, my net earnings jumped by over sixty percent. “For the first time in my life, I paid university fees for my eldest daughter on time, without taking a single bank loan or begging a broker for an advance.” While the multi-million shilling mill stands as the mechanical saviour of the plains, its high efficiency is perfectly matched by a breakthrough in agricultural science by the introduction of theKombokarice variety. Developed to withstand the increasingly unpredictable weather patterns of Western Kenya, Komboka has quickly become the preferred fuel for the new mill. Unlike the traditional, fragileSindanovariety which features tall, delicate stalks that easily fall over and rot when the River Nyando bursts its banks,Kombokavariety boasts a short, sturdy, semi-dwarf architecture. This low profile makes it highly resistant to lodging (falling over) during seasonal flash floods. Under the old system, usingSindanocoupled with village hurlers meant coping with high rates of broken grains, long processing delays, and constant vulnerability to post-harvest mold. The new era pairsKomboka’sstructural flood resilience with the automated mill’s high-speed processing line, guaranteeing premium, whole-head white rice that commands top-tier aromatic prices in urban markets. From a processing perspective, Komboka has an exceptional milling recovery rate. The benefits of the Sh30 million mill extends far beyond the production of clean white rice, the facility has accidentally sparked a secondary gold rush through its industrial by-products. In the old village milling setups, rice husks and bran which were once treated as environmental waste and dumped in massive, burning piles along the roadsides are now cleanly separates and cleaned, opening up fresh economic avenues for local youth and women’s self-help groups. The highly nutritious rice bran is collected and sold at low costs to local entrepreneurs, who use it to manufacture affordable, high-protein animal and poultry feed, boosting the region’s livestock sector. Meanwhile, the thick rice husks are bought by youth groups who use hydraulic presses to compress the waste into eco-friendly briquettes for cooking fuel. These briquettes provide a long-burning, smoke-free alternative to firewood, which is now being sold back to local schools and households thus saving trees, reducing respiratory health hazards, and creating a secondary layer of employment right in the heart of Ahero. Dr. Evans Kipkorir, an agricultural economist and regional food security consultant based in Kisumu notes that the intersection of specialized infrastructure and resilient crop genetics will help rural economies break out of systemic poverty cycle. ”What we are witnessing in Ahero is a textbook example of industrial value addition at the source,” says Dr. Kipkorir. “For decades, Kenyan rice farmers lost an unsustainable portion of their wealth due to inefficient milling. The Sh30 million investment completely eliminates that waste. When you process rice with zero stone contamination and minimal breakage, it immediately outcompetes cheap, sub-standard imports in terms of presentation and consumer trust. This commercial viability keeps millions of shillings circulating right among the people of Kisumu County thus creating more wealth. The factory has also enforced a major upgrade in regional water resource management. Eng. Maurice Onyango, an irrigation infrastructure expert specializing in the Lake Victoria basin, explains how the mill’s predictable processing schedule has optimized the use of the River Nyando. ”Because the automated mill can process large volumes rapidly, farmers can now coordinate their planting and harvesting dates with absolute precision,” Eng. Onyango states. “This predictability allows us to schedule water canal gate rotations perfectly”. We can pump and direct water from the River Nyando to specific sectors exactly when the Komboka crop requires it, eliminating the chaotic water waste and dry-season canal shortages that used to cause widespread crop failures.” The presence of a centralized, corporate-grade mill has also completely reorganized the social fabric of the Kano Plains. In the past, individual smallholders operated in isolation, making them easy targets for predatory buyers. Today, the strict quality standards and structured intake system of the automated mill have forced local farmers to organize themselves into professional digital cooperative societies. Through these smart co-ops, farmers collectively pool their harvests to secure bulk transportation, negotiate better processing rates directly with the mill management, and bypass middlemen entirely. Furthermore, because the mill maintains meticulous, digital records of every delivery, local banks are now using these processing receipts as formal collateral. Farmers can easily access low-interest credit lines to purchase certified seeds and fertilizer, a financial milestone that was completely impossible under the old village milling system. This shift from exhausting manual labor to modern, tech-driven agribusiness is also drawing a new demographic back to the soil. For years, the youth of Kisumu County fled the rural plains, viewing rice farming as a punishing, low-yield activity reserved only for the older generation. But with mechanized tractors preparing the fields, Komboka maturing rapidly in 120 days, and the automated mill handling the heavy processing and packaging, young tech-savvy entrepreneurs are returning to Ahero. They are managing family plots like modern corporations, utilizing mobile money platforms linked directly to the mill’s payout system to track their profits in real time. As evening sets over Ahero, long lines of tractors, trailers and humming vehicles loaded with heavy sacks of freshly harvested paddy line up neatly outside the gates of the Ahero Rice Mill. The steady, rhythmic hum of the heavy machinery serves as an industrial heartbeat for a community that has finally broken free from post-harvest exploitation. Through the mechanical precision of a multi-million shilling automated mill, backed by the resilience of Komboka rice and smart cooperative systems, the farmers of the Kano Plains are no longer just surviving on the land—they are building a powerful commercial empire. The impact of the Ahero Rice Mill extends beyond the production of quality white rice. The facility has created new economic opportunities through the utilization of rice by products that were previously considered waste. “Because the automated mill can process large volumes quickly, farmers can now plan their planting and harvesting periods with greater accuracy,” says Eng. Onyango. “This allows better scheduling of water distribution through canals. Water from River Nyando can be directed to specific areas when the Komboka crop needs it most, reducing wastage and minimizing dry-season shortages.” The establishment of the centralized processing facility has also transformed the way farmers organize themselves. Previously, individual smallholders operated independently, making them vulnerable to exploitation by middlemen. However, the need to meet the mill’s quality requirements has encouraged farmers to form organized cooperative groups. Through these cooperatives, farmers are pooling their harvests, arranging affordable transportation, negotiating better processing arrangements, and accessing markets collectively. The digital record systems used by the mill have further improved farmers’ access to financial services. Records of deliveries and payments provide evidence of production, enabling some farmers to access credit facilities for purchasing certified seeds, fertilizers, and farm inputs. This financial shift has created opportunities that were previously unavailable to many small-scale producers. The modernization of rice farming in Ahero is also attracting young people back into agriculture. For many years, young residents of Kisumu County moved away from rural areas because farming was viewed as a difficult activity with limited returns. However, improved mechanization, better markets, and modern processing facilities are changing that perception. With tractors assisting in land preparation, improved rice varieties maturing faster, and automated milling reducing post-harvest challenges, young entrepreneurs are increasingly investing in rice farming. Some are managing family farms as commercial enterprises, using digital platforms to monitor production, track payments, and improve decision-making. The transformation has positioned rice farming as a viable business opportunity rather than merely a traditional livelihood. As the sun sets over Ahero, the sight of tractors, trailers, and vehicles carrying freshly harvested paddy waiting outside the rice mill reflects a changing agricultural landscape. The steady operation of the automated facility represents a new chapter for farmers who for years struggled with poor processing systems and unfair market conditions. Through modern milling technology, resilient rice varieties such as Komboka, improved irrigation planning, and stronger farmer organizations, the Kano Plains is emerging as a key centre of commercial rice production. The Sh30 million Ahero Rice Mill has become more than a processing facility. It is a symbol of local value addition, economic empowerment, and a renewed future for thousands of farmers who can now earn more from their labour. For the rice farmers of Ahero, the journey is no longer about simply surviving on the land. It is about building a sustainable agribusiness future, one quality grain at a time. By Mabel Keya – Shikukuand Tonaee Bryane

Ematete farmers’ field day promotes climate-smart agriculture innovation. Farmers, agricultural stakeholders, government officials, development partners and agribusiness companies converged at the Ematete Agribusiness Centre in Vihiga County for the fifth Ematete Agribusiness Farmers Field Day to promote climate-smart agriculture, innovation and sustainable agribusiness development. The event, held on Friday under the theme “Enhancing Climate-Smart Agriculture and Agribusiness Innovation,” attracted hundreds of farmers from across the county who interacted with agricultural experts, viewed modern farming technologies and learned practical approaches to improving productivity while adapting to the effects of climate change. The field day was presided over by Vihiga County Chief Officer for Agriculture Betty Mulianga, who urged farmers to embrace climate-smart agricultural practices to safeguard food production amid increasingly unpredictable weather patterns. She said agriculture remains the backbone of Vihiga County’s economy and encouraged farmers to adopt improved seed varieties, efficient water management technologies and modern production methods to increase yields and household incomes. “Climate change is no longer a future challenge but a present reality. We must adopt innovative farming methods that protect the environment while increasing productivity and improving farmers’ incomes,” Mulianga said. She assured farmers that the county government remains committed to strengthening agricultural extension services, supporting agribusiness development and working with development partners to improve food security and economic growth. Mulianga noted that extension officers continue to equip farmers with knowledge on sustainable farming practices, soil conservation, crop diversification and climate adaptation to help them cope with changing weather conditions. Mwibona Ward Member of the County Assembly Zakayo Manyasa urged residents to embrace commercial agriculture by viewing farming as a business rather than a subsistence activity. He said equipping farmers with modern knowledge, technologies and entrepreneurial skills would create employment opportunities, improve household incomes and strengthen food security within the county. Manyasa challenged young people to venture into agribusiness, saying agriculture offers numerous opportunities for wealth creation through crop production, livestock farming, value addition and agricultural marketing. The event featured exhibitions by farmers, agribusiness companies and agricultural organisations showcasing improved crop varieties, livestock products, certified seeds, farm machinery, irrigation technologies, value-added agricultural products and climate-smart farming innovations. Farmers also demonstrated practical farming techniques, giving participants an opportunity to observe and learn best practices that can be replicated to improve productivity and resilience on their own farms. The Cereals Growers Association (CGA), led by Benson Omukhago, highlighted its efforts to strengthen cereal production through farmer training, access to quality farm inputs, collective marketing and promotion of climate-smart agricultural practices. Omukhago encouraged farmers to adopt improved cereal production technologies, diversify their farming enterprises and strengthen producer organisations to enhance bargaining power and improve market access. He said empowering farmers with technical knowledge and reliable markets is essential for building resilient and profitable agricultural value chains capable of withstanding climate-related challenges. Seed Co representatives, led by Benjamin Kidigi, exhibited a range of certified and improved seed varieties developed to help farmers increase productivity and adapt to changing climatic conditions. Kidigi educated farmers on the importance of using certified seeds, observing proper crop management practices and selecting crop varieties suited to different ecological zones to maximise yields. He urged farmers to embrace improved seed technologies as an effective way of increasing food production, enhancing household food security and improving farm profitability. The field day also strengthened partnerships between farmers, government agencies, private companies, financial institutions and agricultural organisations through discussions on market access, sustainable agriculture, climate resilience and agribusiness innovation. Participants expressed appreciation for the opportunity to interact directly with experts and exhibitors, saying the event equipped them with practical knowledge, new technologies and market information that would help improve farm productivity and increase household incomes. The event concluded with renewed calls for sustained collaboration among government, development partners, research institutions, private sector players and farming communities to accelerate agricultural transformation, strengthen climate resilience and promote sustainable food production in Vihiga County. By Henry Ananda and Kelly Barasa

Collaboration key to improving education standards, stakeholders told. Political leaders, school managers, teachers, parents and communities have been urged to strengthen collaboration to improve education standards and ensure learners are equipped with the knowledge and skills required to thrive in a rapidly changing world. Education stakeholders say while government policies provide the framework for learning, sustained partnerships among leaders, schools and communities are essential for translating policy into improved infrastructure, better learning environments and stronger academic performance. In Tinderet Sub-County, Nandi County, this collaborative approach is gaining momentum through regular engagements between area Member of Parliament Julius Melly and managers of learning institutions. Over the past few weeks, the legislator has visited Fr. Boyle Kabalebo Senior School, Tinderet Technical and Vocational Training College (TVTC) at Sigoria and Chemamul Senior School, where discussions focused on infrastructure development, quality education and the implementation of the Competency-Based Education (CBE) programme. Education experts say such engagements demonstrate the importance of leaders working closely with schools to identify development priorities, mobilise resources and monitor ongoing projects. They note that schools benefit when leaders move beyond ceremonial visits and instead engage administrators on practical solutions to challenges affecting teaching and learning. The interactions also promote accountability in the utilisation of public resources while assuring communities that education remains central to national development. During his visit to Fr. Boyle Kabalebo Senior School, Melly inspected infrastructure projects funded through the National Government Constituencies Development Fund (NG-CDF). He said the government and local leaders must continue investing in quality learning facilities to create an environment where students can excel academically. “Our commitment is to ensure that every learner studies in a conducive environment. Education is the greatest equaliser, and we shall continue investing in classrooms, laboratories and other facilities through the NG-CDF so that our children can compete with the best anywhere in the country,” he said. The legislator urged parents to remain actively involved in the education of their children by supporting teachers in nurturing discipline, monitoring academic progress and encouraging regular school attendance. He also challenged school managers and boards of management to ensure prudent utilisation of public funds so that every development project delivers value to learners. Education stakeholders observed that government funding alone cannot meet all the needs of schools and that partnerships involving communities, leaders and development partners are necessary to bridge existing gaps. The same message featured prominently during Melly’s visit to Tinderet Technical and Vocational Training College at Sigoria, where he inspected a newly completed one-storey tuition block ahead of the commissioning of a modern Electrical and Electronics Engineering workshop. The institution is among the technical training centres expected to play a key role in equipping young people with practical skills aligned to the needs of industry and the labour market. Addressing tutors, administrators and students, Melly encouraged young people to embrace Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET), saying Kenya’s economic transformation depends on a skilled workforce capable of supporting industrial growth and innovation. “Our young people require employable skills that respond to the changing labour market. Strengthening our technical institutions will empower graduates to create jobs, support industries and contribute meaningfully to the country’s economic growth,” he said. The MP pledged continued support for expanding infrastructure at the institution to enable more students from Tinderet and neighbouring areas to access affordable, quality technical education. Education experts say collaboration between political leaders and TVET institutions has the potential to improve access to modern workshops, specialised equipment and student support programmes, thereby producing graduates with competitive skills. Melly later visited Chemamul Senior School, where discussions centred on preparations for the implementation of the Competency-Based Education programme at the senior school level. Stakeholders noted that the transition to senior school under the new curriculum has created additional demands for classrooms, science laboratories, workshops, learning materials and qualified teaching staff. Addressing members of the school management and Board of Management, the legislator said successful implementation of the education reforms would depend on sustained cooperation among all stakeholders. “The Competency-Based Education programme calls for adequate infrastructure, teaching resources and close collaboration among all stakeholders. We cannot leave schools to shoulder this responsibility alone. Leaders, teachers, parents and communities must work together to ensure our learners receive quality education,” he said. He reaffirmed his commitment to supporting the construction of additional facilities required to accommodate the growing number of learners joining senior schools under the CBE system. Teachers welcomed the engagements, saying they provide an opportunity to present institutional priorities directly to policymakers and seek timely interventions before challenges affect learning outcomes. Education analysts observed that communities where leaders maintain close working relationships with schools often record faster implementation of development projects, stronger accountability and increased public confidence in the education sector. Parents were also reminded that their responsibility extends beyond paying school fees to supporting discipline, participating in school development initiatives and maintaining close communication with teachers. Stakeholders said the combined efforts of committed teachers, supportive parents, responsive leaders and active communities create an environment in which learners can realise their full potential. The experiences at Fr. Boyle Kabalebo Senior School, Tinderet TVTC and Chemamul Senior School illustrate that improving education standards is a shared responsibility requiring sustained partnerships among government, political leaders, school managers, parents, development partners and local communities. By Sammy Mwibanda

Government promotes horticulture farming to boost farmers’ incomes. Farmers in Southern Nyanza have been encouraged to embrace horticulture farming as a profitable venture capable of improving household incomes and creating sustainable livelihoods. Former Horticulture Development Authority (HCDA) official and horticulture expert John Rono said crops such as passion fruits, vegetables and tomatoes provide farmers with reliable earnings because they generate income on a daily or weekly basis. Speaking during a passion fruit farming exhibition at Ayego Passion Fruits Groups Farm, Rono said horticultural produce has ready markets locally and internationally throughout the year, unlike some traditional crops whose returns are affected by market fluctuations. He noted that many farmers in the region have continued to rely heavily on maize and sugarcane despite facing persistent challenges associated with the two crops. Rono expressed concern that horticulture production in the region remains low because nearly 99 per cent of farmers concentrate on large-scale maize and sugarcane farming. “Horticulture fruits have a wider market which spreads from Nairobi to Kampala in neighbouring Uganda. Farmers should take advantage of this opportunity by putting more land under fruit and vegetable production,” he told farmers attending the two-day exhibition sponsored by AMPATH. He said the exhibition provided farmers with an opportunity to learn modern horticulture farming technologies, including irrigation, greenhouse farming and shade-net production. Rono urged farmers to diversify their agricultural activities by adopting high-value crops that can provide consistent income and reduce dependence on traditional crops. He added that increased production of fruits and vegetables in Southern Nyanza would help reduce reliance on supplies from other regions and create opportunities for local farmers. Tomatoes, passion fruits and other horticultural products continue to have strong demand in markets across the country, but production in the region remains insufficient. Farmers were encouraged to take advantage of available technologies and market opportunities to transform horticulture into a major source of income and economic growth. By George Agimba

Governor Mutai orders crackdown on unlicensed milk vendors. Kericho Governor Dr. Erick Mutai has ordered an immediate crackdown on unlicensed raw milk vendors and brokers, declaring that the purchase, aggregation and distribution of raw milk outside the county’s licensing framework is illegal. The governor said the county government would intensify enforcement against illegal milk aggregators to protect dairy farmers from exploitation and ensure milk is marketed through licensed channels. He noted that strengthening cooperative societies remains central to the county’s strategy to improve farmers’ earnings by eliminating middlemen who deny producers fair returns. Dr. Mutai said the county would continue investing in the dairy sector through milk cooling plants, feed mixers, artificial insemination services and Enterprise Development Programme (EDP) grants to registered cooperative societies. He said the interventions are intended to increase milk production, improve quality, promote value addition and enable farmers to earn higher incomes. “Our focus is to build strong cooperative societies that can collect, process and market farmers’ milk competitively. We will continue investing in cooling infrastructure, animal feeds, quality breeding and farmer empowerment because a stronger dairy sector translates into better household incomes, more jobs for our youth and sustained economic growth for Kericho,” said Dr. Mutai. The governor made the remarks during the funeral service of the late schoolteacher and farmer Ann Chebochok at the Kericho Golf Club Grounds on Friday. Besides addressing dairy sector reforms, Dr. Mutai called for urgent measures to curb the rising number of road fatalities, saying improved highways must be accompanied by enhanced road safety interventions. He urged the national government to fast-track the installation of speed cameras, improve hazardous sections of roads, strengthen enforcement of traffic laws and intensify public awareness campaigns aimed at reducing accidents and protecting road users. “Every life lost on our roads is a reminder that we must do more. We need a combination of better road designs, strict enforcement of traffic regulations and the use of technology such as speed monitoring systems to prevent reckless driving and save lives,” he said. Chebochok, the sister of former Bomet Governor and current Judicial Service Commission Vice Chairperson Isaac Ruto, died in a road accident along Nairobi’s Southern Bypass. According to her family, the accident occurred a few minutes before 6:00 a.m. A post-mortem examination established that she succumbed to severe internal organ injuries sustained in the crash. Her daughter, who was travelling with her, survived the accident after sustaining minor injuries and was discharged after receiving medical attention. Dr. Mutai described Chebochok as a dedicated teacher, accomplished farmer and community leader whose commitment to agriculture and public service positively impacted many lives. He said continued support for farmers and stronger agricultural cooperatives would help preserve the legacy of hardworking producers like her while promoting sustainable economic development in the county. The funeral service brought together national and county leaders, including Principal Secretary for the State Department for Water and Sanitation Julius Korir, Bomet Governor Prof. Hillary Barchok, Kericho Woman Representative Beatrice Kemei, Isaac Ruto, family members, friends and hundreds of mourners who gathered to celebrate Chebochok’s life, honour her contribution to society and stand with her family during the difficult period. By Kelox Mutai

Mt Kenya East leaders back Ruto-Kindiki ticket in 2027. Public Service Cabinet Secretary Geoffrey Ruku has said leaders allied to the Kenya Kwanza administration in Mt Kenya East will support President William Ruto and Deputy President Kithure Kindiki in the 2027 General Election, citing ongoing government development projects in the region. Speaking during an academic day at Kirindine Day Secondary School in Igembe South on Friday, Ruku said the government remains focused on implementing development programmes in education, infrastructure and agriculture. He said the administration has allocated resources to support schools through capitation and improve access to quality education. Ruku also noted that the region currently holds a prominent position in national leadership and called on residents to remain united as the government continues implementing its development agenda. He urged residents to assess leaders based on the development initiatives undertaken in their areas. Igembe South MP John Paul Mwirigi said the constituency has benefited from several national government projects, including the establishment of a Huduma Centre, construction of a new police station, creation of Akachiu Sub-county, allocation of Sh50 million for government infrastructure and Sh17 million for the construction of Kiegoi–Antubochiu Sub-county offices, which he said are expected to begin in August. Mwirigi also said the government’s recruitment of teachers has helped improve staffing levels in public schools and enhanced access to education. Buuri MP Mugambi Rindikiri also expressed support for the Kenya Kwanza administration, saying the government has implemented development projects in various parts of the region. He encouraged residents to continue supporting development initiatives. The leaders made the remarks as political activities continue to gather momentum in the Mt. Kenya region ahead of the 2027 General Election. By Kamanja Maeria

Diversification pays off as North Rift maize farmers count losses. As prolonged dry spells continue to slash maize production across the North Rift, a Uasin Gishu farmer who shifted to high-value, climate-resilient crops is earning nearly Sh1 million annually, offering a practical example of how diversification can cushion farmers against climate change and unstable markets. David Kwambai, 71, of Kapsoen Village in Moiben Sub-county, abandoned reliance on maize and invested in coffee, avocado and macadamia farming, transforming his four-acre farm into a profitable agribusiness while many maize growers grapple with declining yields. His success comes as agricultural experts and regional leaders urge farmers to reduce dependence on maize by embracing crops that are more resilient to changing weather patterns and command better market prices. Kwambai told the Kenya News Agency (KNA) that he began growing coffee in 2015 with about 100 trees before gradually expanding to about 2,000 trees after realizing the crop generated better returns than maize. “I started coffee farming in 2015 with about 100 trees, and over time I increased the number to around 2,000. Although prices were not very good in the beginning, I realized coffee was still more profitable than maize,” he said. He said his coffee harvest initially averaged between 300 and 400 kilograms but is expected to exceed 1,000 kilograms this season due to improved farm management and favourable prices. Kwambai sold last year’s coffee through a cooperative society at about Sh700 per kilogram, describing cooperative marketing as a key factor in improving farmers’ incomes. “Coffee harvesting takes about two to three months, but with good care, the returns are worth it,” he said, although he identified coffee berry disease as his biggest production challenge. Seeking to spread risk, the farmer later ventured into avocado and macadamia farming after losses in cabbage and passion fruit production caused by disease outbreaks and poor markets. His 500 avocado trees, planted on two acres, produce between 50 and 80 kilograms of fruit per tree, with the produce selling at an average of Sh110 per kilogram. “Avocado farming is doing very well because of export demand. We harvest about three times a year, giving us a steady source of income,” he said. Kwambai has also embraced sustainable farming practices by producing compost from fallen avocado leaves, cow dung and urea to improve soil fertility and reduce production costs. However, he cited pests, diseases, cold weather and inadequate irrigation water as the major constraints affecting avocado production. His macadamia enterprise is also showing promising returns. Having planted the crop in 2018, he harvested about 300 kilograms of nuts last year and sold them at Sh150 per kilogram. “This year I expect even better yields. Macadamia is a long-term investment, but it pays off,” he said. Beyond crop production, Kwambai practices apiculture and livestock farming to diversify his income further. He keeps 10 beehives, six of which are active, producing up to 200 kilograms of honey every three to four months depending on weather conditions. He also rears dairy cows and goats, which provide additional income while supplying manure used to enrich soil fertility on the farm. Although he has access to water from a drilled source, Kwambai said he has not fully adopted irrigation, noting that expanding irrigation would significantly improve productivity during prolonged dry spells. He identified marketing as another challenge facing farmers, saying coffee growers benefit from cooperative marketing structures while avocado farmers largely depend on brokers because of inadequate storage and cooling facilities. “We need proper storage and cooling plants to reduce post-harvest losses, especially for avocados, which are highly perishable,” he said, adding that farmers are considering forming cooperatives to strengthen their bargaining power. Kwambai appealed to the county and national governments to subsidize farm inputs and deploy more agricultural extension officers to train farmers on modern production methods, soil testing and climate-smart agriculture. He also encouraged young people to embrace agriculture as a business, saying farming can generate sustainable livelihoods when managed professionally. “Even at my age, I am still actively farming and employing young people. Agriculture has great potential if farmers embrace the right crops,” he said. His experience reflects growing calls for North Rift farmers to diversify into drought-tolerant, high-value enterprises as erratic rainfall and prolonged dry spells continue to undermine conventional maize production. Thousands of maize farmers across the region are experiencing reduced yields because of changing weather patterns, highlighting the risks of relying on a single crop and reinforcing the importance of climate-smart agriculture, improved market access and enterprise diversification in building resilient farming systems. By Fredrick Maritim

Nakuru County strengthens dairy subsector. The County Government of Nakuru has pledged to continue strengthening the dairy sector by investing in projects that help farmers reduce post-harvest losses and increase their incomes. According to County Executive Committee Member (CECM) for Agriculture, Livestock and Fisheries Mr Leonard Bor, through such programmes, the devolved unit’s administration remains committed to building a stronger and more profitable dairy sector for the region’s farmers. Mr. Bor pointed out that the dairy value chain is a vital economic pillar, supporting millions of livelihoods from farmers and transporters to processors, retailers and consumers. He said the interventions are part of Governor Susan Kihika’s administration’s efforts to revitalize the dairy sector in the country aimed at boosting value addition and creating sustainable jobs. “We are actively strengthening the dairy value chain to boost productivity, minimize post-harvest losses, and increase farmers’ incomes. Key initiatives include milk cooler distributions, training farmers on animal feed formulation, vaccination drives and livestock disease surveillance among other measures,” stated the CECM. He spoke at the county offices in Nakuru Town during a meeting with officials of the Elburgon Progressive Cooperative Society who were accompanied by the director of the Poland–East Africa Economic Foundation, Mr. Robert Zduńczyk. Mr Bor disclosed that his department was crafting regional and international partnerships aimed at equipping farmers with modern dairy production skills, improve access to advanced farming technologies and enhance the competitiveness of cooperative societies, in a move expected to increase milk production and boost household incomes. Mr. Bor indicated that the county government has consistently supported investment in farmer training, improved breeding technologies and cold-chain infrastructure to enhance milk quality, increase production and improve the competitiveness of Kenyan dairy products in regional and international markets. He further noted that strengthening cooperative societies through technical training and international partnerships enables farmers to access new technologies, improve farm management practices and increase profitability while creating employment opportunities for young people in agriculture. The CECM added that the devolved unit’s administration had partnered with the Poland–East Africa Economic Foundation to facilitate knowledge exchange, farmer training and access to modern agricultural machinery through cooperative societies. The collaboration is aimed at building farmers’ capacity to adopt climate-smart and commercially viable dairy farming practices while improving productivity across the county. Bor said the County government was working closely with the national government towards strengthening milk aggregation, processing and market access through key milk collection centres. He further called for collective support to strengthen the dairy value chain as a pathway to reducing poverty and creating jobs and reiterated the County Government’s commitment to working with farmers through capacity building and improved market access both locally and internationally. Official statistics indicate that nationally, livestock contributes 50 percent of Agricultural Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and over 10 percent of the National GDP. Dairy production is the largest contributor to the livestock GDP. The statistics reveal that the dairy sub-sector yields about Sh237 billion annually and that Kenya is one of the leading countries in dairy cattle production in Africa. Mr Bor stated that the industry is on an upward trajectory with an estimated growth rate of 3 percent to 4 percent per year adding that the Kenya Kwanza administration recognizes dairy value chain as one of the main sources of household incomes and a crucial contributor to food security. Vision 2030 which has been adopted as a new model for Kenya’s development, emphasizes the enhancement of dairy productivity as key to increasing incomes, food security and nutrition. The Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock Development developed a Dairy Master Plan 2010– 2030, and Kenya Dairy Industry Transformation Strategy & Investment Plan 2022-2032, developed by the Kenya Dairy Board, which currently guides the dairy industry. Mr. Bor said the County government is striving to make the dairy subsector one of the leading subsectors in socio-economic development through production, value addition and marketing. This, he added, is being done by mobilizing and working with all stakeholders and development partners as the county seeks to maximize the utilization of all available opportunities and resources for the benefit of the entire region. The partnership with Poland–East Africa Economic Foundation, the CECM noted, would provide dairy farmers with practical knowledge and exposure to modern farming technologies that can improve efficiency, increase milk yields and strengthen the county’s dairy value chain. He pointed out that members of the Elburgon Progressive Cooperative Society would participate in an exchange programme where they will receive hands-on training in feed and forage formulation, modern dairy production techniques and the use of mechanized farm equipment. Mr. Bor called on beneficiaries of the partnership to share the skills acquired with other farmer groups and cooperatives to ensure the benefits of the programme reach more dairy producers across the county. The CECM said knowledge transfer and collaboration among cooperatives remains essential in building a resilient and sustainable dairy industry capable of competing in local and international markets. He said the partnership complements the County Government’s ongoing efforts to modernize dairy farming through subsidized artificial insemination (AI) services, improved breeding programmes and investment in milk handling infrastructure. “The county has also supplied milk coolers to several dairy cooperatives, including Elburgon Progressive Cooperative Society, to improve milk quality, reduce post-harvest losses and increase farmers’ earnings,” he observed. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), dairy farming plays a critical role in improving rural livelihoods by providing regular household income, creating employment and enhancing food and nutrition security. FAO notes that improved animal genetics, quality feeds and farmer training are among the most effective interventions for increasing milk productivity. The International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) observes that knowledge exchange and adoption of modern livestock technologies enable smallholder farmers to improve productivity while strengthening resilience to climate change and fluctuating market conditions. In Kenya, the dairy industry is one of the country’s leading agricultural sub-sectors. According to the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS), livestock contributes significantly to agricultural GDP, with dairy farming supporting the livelihoods of millions of Kenyans directly and indirectly through production, processing, transportation and marketing. The State Department for Livestock Development estimates that Kenya produces more than 5 billion litres of milk annually, making it one of Africa’s leading milk producers. The sector supports over 1.8 million smallholder dairy farmers, with cooperatives playing a vital role in milk collection, value addition and market access. For Nakuru farmers, the collaboration is expected to improve dairy productivity, promote the adoption of modern farming practices, strengthen cooperative societies and expand market opportunities, ultimately increasing household incomes and contributing to Kenya’s food security and economic growth. By Jane Ngugi and Jefther Afuyo

Industry-led apprenticeships offer solution to skills gap, unemployment. Industry-led apprenticeship programmes can significantly improve business productivity while providing a practical solution to youth unemployment in Kenya, according to a new study on skills development. The Return on Investment (ROI) Study on the PropelA Dual Apprenticeship Programme found that companies investing in workforce skills development record an average 30 per cent Return on Training Investment (ROTI), generate approximately Sh2 million in net value per company and recover their investment within three years. The independent study, conducted by Orange & Teal on behalf of Swisscontact, revealed that nearly 87 per cent of the value created through apprenticeship programmes comes from increased apprentice productivity, demonstrating the economic benefits of investing in practical skills training. The findings were unveiled during the PropelA Business Impact and Investment Insights Breakfast in Nairobi, bringing together government officials, private sector leaders, development partners and workforce development stakeholders to discuss strategies for addressing skills shortages and improving youth employment. Swisscontact Kenya Country Director Sharon Mosin said the findings demonstrate that skills development should be viewed as an economic investment rather than merely a social intervention. “Skills are economic infrastructure that drive productivity, competitiveness and growth. When businesses invest in skills, they are investing in their own future,” said Mosin. She said stronger partnerships between industry and training institutions were necessary to address the mismatch between skills possessed by graduates and those required by employers. The Kenya Association of Manufacturers (KAM) urged more employers to adopt demand-driven training models, saying such programmes have delivered measurable returns while opening employment opportunities for young people. KAM Chief Executive Officer Tobias Alando said collaboration with Swisscontact through the PropelA programme has trained more than 1,500 young people, facilitated employment for over 1,260 graduates, supported eight industry-led curriculum reviews and equipped 710 youth with entrepreneurship and financial literacy skills. Alando called for stronger collaboration among industry players, training institutions and government agencies while urging reforms to the National Industrial Training Authority (NITA) levy framework to encourage increased private sector participation in workforce development. NITA Manager for Industrial Training Development Musa Opuk said the government had strengthened work-based learning approaches to address concerns raised by employers over graduates lacking adequate practical skills. He explained that the dual apprenticeship model enables trainees to spend 70 per cent of their training period in industry and 30 per cent in learning institutions, allowing them to gain hands-on experience while pursuing recognised Level 5 and Level 6 qualifications under the Kenya National Qualifications Framework. Opuk said more than 80 per cent of apprentices are absorbed into employment after completing their training, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining classroom instruction with workplace exposure. He added that NITA is reviewing the industrial training levy framework to provide greater incentives for employers, including subsidised training opportunities and tax incentives for firms that support apprenticeship programmes. The government is also introducing a graduate apprenticeship programme under which employers hiring graduate apprentices will benefit from tax deductions. “Employers who pay wages to graduate apprentices will be eligible for a tax deduction of up to 50 per cent of the wages paid,” said Opuk. He commended businesses that have embraced apprenticeship programmes, saying their investment in skills development was contributing to youth empowerment and economic growth. Nicholas Komu, Director at Realtech Plumbers Ltd., said the company joined the PropelA Dual Apprenticeship Programme after identifying its potential to bridge the skills gap in the construction sector through a combination of classroom learning and workplace training. Komu said the plumbing industry had experienced a shortage of skilled technicians due to declining enrolment in technical institutions and economic challenges experienced in previous decades, forcing many companies to recruit and train inexperienced workers internally. “The plumbing industry had faced a shortage of skilled technicians for years due to low enrollment in technical institutions and an economic slowdown in the 1990s, forcing many firms to recruit and train inexperienced workers on the job,” he said. He added that the company has enrolled apprentices in two cohorts, with trainees demonstrating improved competence, confidence and workplace readiness. Following the success of the programme, Komu said Realtech Plumbers plans to increase the number of apprentices recruited in the next cohort and encouraged more employers to embrace apprenticeship models. The study also highlighted the benefits that small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) can gain through improved productivity, competitiveness and access to skilled workers. Initially introduced in electrical and plumbing trades, the PropelA programme has expanded to welding, lift and escalator maintenance, maintenance services and selected hospitality occupations. The programme has potential for adoption in other sectors including manufacturing, energy, transport and agribusiness, where demand for skilled workers continues to grow. Since its launch in 2023, PropelA has partnered with more than 70 companies, trained over 400 apprentices and achieved an employment rate of more than 80 per cent. Stakeholders said the success of the programme demonstrates the potential of work-based learning to strengthen enterprise performance, reduce youth unemployment and create sustainable career pathways for young people. By Wangari Ndirangu

Religious leaders condemn political violence. Religious leaders under the Spiritual Churches Council of Kenya have strongly condemned the recent incident of political violence reported in Keumbu, Kisii County on July 3, 2026, where goons allegedly attacked the Linda Mwananchi convoy. Speaking in Migori Town, the clergy, led by Dick Okuku, urged politicians to exercise tolerance and conduct peaceful campaigns while cautioning young people against being manipulated into engaging in violence for political interests. “We are urging our Gen Zs and other youths to desist from being used and manipulated by the political class to settle their political scores”, said Okuku. The church leaders, however, commended Migori County political leadership for embracing peaceful coexistence, noting that the county has witnessed a significant reduction in political violence compared to the past. They reaffirmed their commitment to working with political leaders, the public, and other stakeholders to promote peace, unity, and issue-based politics as the country prepares for the upcoming General Election. “We are now 13 months to the next general elections, and we urge both the county and national leaders to exercise utmost political restraint, show respect, maintain peace and unity to have a prosperous country,” said Okuku. Mary Robi, also a clergy member, explained that as clergies, they will continue praying for the nation to achieve a peaceful election for the betterment of society. She urged the youth to remain focused and achieve what they want through the ballot instead of being allowed to be used cheaply by the political class. Robi noted that it is so painful to lose a child through political violence, adding that every life is sacred. She commended the Migori political class for showing great restraint and political tolerance in recent weeks and urged them to continue promoting peace and unity for the advancement of the socio-political and economic agendas. by Makokha Khaoya

Kenya safe and stable for tourists and investors, declare coastal leaders. Leaders from the coastal region have assured tourists and investors that Kenya in general and the coastal region in particular is a safe destination. Tourism is the economic backbone of Mombasa, Kwale, Kilifi and Lamu counties and supports local livelihoods, drives the hospitality sector, and stimulates related industries like agriculture and transport. The leaders have condemned recent statements by former deputy president Rigathi Gachagua that tourists and investors should avoid the country in the runup to the 2027 general election. Gachagua the Democracy for Citizens Party (DCP) leader has urged tourists and investors to stay away from Kenya, citing rising insecurity that he blamed squarely on the national government. They said the tourism sector should not remain stagnant simply because the country is hurtling towards a high-stake general election. The leaders were speaking in Mombasa after a high-level consultative meeting to discuss the future of the Coast region and strengthen collaboration towards sustainable economic growth and shared prosperity. Led by Cabinet Secretaries Hassan Joho (Mining, Blue Economy and Maritime Affairs) and Salim Mvurya (Youth Affairs, Creative Economy and Sports), the leaders said politicians should desist from issuing travel advisories and precautions to visitors and investors. Others were Senate Speaker Amason Kingi, Governors Abdulswamad Shariff Nassir (Mombasa), Gideon Mung’aro (Kilifi) and Issa Timamy (Lamu), senators Mohamed Faki (Mombasa) and Stewart Madzayo (Kilifi) and a host of MPs. Joho, Mvurya and Kingi are also past two-term governors of Mombasa, Kwale and Kilifi counties. CS Joho said Gachagua’s remarks that tourists and investors should stay away from Kenya over insecurity concerns was reckless and economic sabotage. He said Kenya has built a strong international reputation through its wildlife, white sandy beaches, rich culture and hospitality noting that negative portrayals could discourage potential visitors. “As leaders from the coast region, we condemn in the strongest terms possible the reckless and unfortunate remarks made by Gachagua, which appear calculated to undermine the tourism sector, the lifeblood of our regional economy, and discourage investment in the coast,” said Joho. Joho said such statements are not only irresponsible but also detrimental to the livelihoods of millions of people who depend directly and indirectly on tourism, hospitality, transport, trade and other sectors driven by a thriving coastal economy. He said for decades there have been individuals who have viewed the coastal region through the lens of ‘’exclusion and political expediency often seeking to destabilize its tourism driven economy for selfish political gains. “This pattern of divisive politics has, for decades, denied our people the opportunities and recognition they deserve,” he said, adding that the remarks come at a time when the national government is attempting to attract more visitors. He went on ‘our people will no longer be distracted by politics of fear, division or economic sabotage’. Joho said coastal leaders are united in safeguarding the fragile tourism industry, protecting jobs and creating an enabling environment that welcomes local and foreign investors. CS Joho says it’s unfortunate that the remarks come in the backdrop of a recent announcement by Nigerian tycoon Ali Dankote that he is set to put up a $17 billion (Sh2.2 trillion) mega oil refinery in Lamu. Dangote’s refinery is projected to process about 700,000 barrels per day, making it the largest oil refinery in East Africa. CS Mvurya said the unfortunate remarks by the former Deputy President came at a time local leaders were deliberating on how best to work together to fully exploit the region’s immense potential in tourism and the blue economy sector with a view to occasioning job creation, poverty eradication and improved socio-economic status. “We should all be committed to a concerted effort to create an enabling environment conducive to sustainable tourism development,” said Mvurya. Governor Nassir said the devolved governments in the coastal region are involved in a new strategy of attracting tourists from outside European nations that have traditionally been major sources of visitors. “We are working closely with global airlines in a bid to open direct flights through open sky policy,” he said. He said open sky policy allows international airlines to operate direct flights into Moi International Airport in Mombasa. “This initiative bypasses the need for tourists to connect through Nairobi, significantly easing travel and driving tourism growth in the coastal region,” he said. Airlines like Ethiopian Airlines, Flydubai, and various charter flights already utilize direct routes, bringing tourists closer to coastal destinations. He said leaders should champion keeping the tourism sector insulated from partisan politics to drive economic growth. Kilifi Governor Gideon Mung’aro said the utterances by Gachagua are irresponsible, undermine the country’s international reputation, and threaten the livelihoods of millions of Kenyans who depend on the tourism sector. “Tourism remains a key economic pillar for the coast, and any attempt to sabotage it is an attack on our economy, businesses, and families,” said Mung’aro. According to the ministry of tourism the country recorded about 2.7 million international tourist arrivals in 2025. The national government is targeting five million international arrivals by 2028, a goal that depends on sustaining global confidence in Kenya as a safe, secure and attractive destination. By Hussein Abdullahi

Man sentenced to life imprisonment for defiling toddler. By S, KNA A father of eight who pleaded not guilty to defiling his 17- months- old niece at his house has been jailed for life by a Kericho court. Kericho Senior Resident Magistrate Japhet Bii found Justus Kipsigei Cheruiyot, 46, guilty of defiling the toddler in his house on 1 May 2025 at Chesingoro village in Bureti sub-county within Kericho County. Cheruiyot was also charged with an alternative charge of committing an indecent act with the young child to which he also pleaded not guilty. The prosecution produced six witnesses, all who gave corroborating evidence against the accused. The court heard that on 1, May 2025, the toddler’s mother at around 10.20am, was woken up from her nap by her four- year- old daughter with information that her 17- months- old sibling was being killed by the accused whom he had taken to his house while armed with a knife. The child’s mother on rushing out of her house, met the accused who is her brother fleeing as he dropped her crying toddler to the ground. The mother found her naked child having lost consciousness with blood oozing from her genitals and mouth. She took her toddler to Kapkatet sub-county hospital for treatment where they were brought to Kericho Referral Hospital in an ambulance and the child was taken for surgery and admitted at the facility for 12 days. The matter was reported to Litein police station and the accused was arrested at around 5pm on May 1, 2025. A clinical officer who examined the minor told the court that indeed the toddler had been defiled. A P3 form and laboratory reports tabled before the court indicated that the hymen had been freshly torn and there was bleeding of her private parts. Sexual activity had taken place with penetration as observed with the broken hymen further confirming the defilement charge. A birth certificate was tabled before the court revealing the toddler was indeed 17- months- old at the time of the heinous ordeal. In his defence, the accused gave a sworn testimony and denied committing the offence. He told the court that he did not know what had happened that day. Cheruiyot added that he was arrested and taken to the police station where he was informed that he had defiled a child. He further told the court that the child was usually in the company of her mother and there was no way he would have defiled his niece. In mitigation, the accused pleaded for leniency asking for a non-custodial sentence as he had eight children who depended on him but the magistrate found him guilty and ordered that he serves life imprisonment. “I have considered the mitigation. I have also considered the circumstances which the offense was committed. The accused person committed a beastly act upon a child of tender age that was savage. It is more disturbing that the child belongs to the accused sister who lives in the same compound. From the foregoing, I find that the elements required to prove a case as this have been properly established. There was penetration of a minor by the accused person. The case against him has properly been proved. The accused is hereby found guilty as charged. He is consequently convicted under section 215 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cap 75) laws of Kenya.” Bii ruled. The convict was reminded of the right to appeal the sentence within 14 days if dissatisfied.

St. Mary’s Mission Hospital, Kakamega paid Sh98 dues. By G, KNA Cabinet Secretary for Health Aden Duale has announced release of Sh98 million owed to the troubled St. Mary’s Mission Hospital in Mumias, Kakamega county paving way for its reopening. Speaking to the press outside the Kakamega County Governor offices after a meeting, Duale also announced that the government will in the next two weeks’ pay Kakamega County Sh100 million being part of the claims from SHA and that further reimbursements will be done once the ongoing verification of all claims is concluded. “By 14th of this week, the date SHA pays reimbursements, we shall pay Kakamega county Sh100 million and the remaining balances to be paid out once verification of all claims are concluded,” he added. Duale said the Ministry has put in place an AI Powered detection system that monitors every transaction real time, detecting suspicious patterns and blocking fraudulent claims. On St. Mary Mission hospital is Mumias run by the Kakamega Catholic Dioceses, ceased operations last month due to financial issues and alleged non-remittance of funds by the Ministry of Health. However, Duale said the hospital has since December last year to August this year, been reimbursed a total of Sh98 million. The CS said the hospital will receive another reimbursement of Sh14.3 million in the next two weeks, but said they have agreed with Bishop Joseph Obanyi of Kakamega Diocese on how the remaining balances will be cleared, once verification is concluded. “So from where we sit St, Mary’s hospital has not been closed by SHA, nor by the regulator Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentist council, or the Digital Health Agency that controls the system and their license valid to operate. The CS said on reopening of the health facility, he will preside over a donation of a consignment of drugs from the government and a medical camp at the facility for area residents,” he added. “Those who are peddling rumors in funerals and to use St. Mary’s hospital for political mileage to look for something else to talk about”, he said, in an apparent reference to some politicians who have been calling for his resignation over non-remittance of claims to health facilities countrywide. Duale said the Ministry of Health will in the next two weeks unveil a Digital Tracking System in all public health facilities to curb theft of medical commodities. “We have put in place a water tight solid system to ensure that no staff can steal any medical commodities, not even a Panadol and the system will be operational in all public health institutions in two weeks’ time.” he added. Kakamega Diocese Bishop Joseph Obanyi, who also addressed the media said that they had had fruitful discussion with the CS and his team and confirmed that St. Mary’s Mission hospital had received a total Sh98,671,567 Million from SHA since December last year to August this year. “We have pending claims of Sh35 million that we expect to receive from SHA which will help us clear the arrears for workers’ pay,” he said. “We also have pending Sh10 million still being verified by SHA and will continue engaging,” said Bishop Obanyi. The Bishop said strike of workers at the health facility that led for ceasing of medical services was due to accruing salary arrears of 3 months from defunct National Health Insurance FUND (NHIF), which stands at Sh143 million. Bishop Obanyi added that once they receive another pending claim of about Sh14 million, when the necessary documentation and verification is concluded in the next two weeks, then St. Mary’s Mission Hospital will engage the workers to resume work. Kakamega Governor Fernandez Barasa said Kakamega County has registered a total of 800,000 people under SHA against its target of 1.8 Million people “We have embarked on a serious registration exercise to register the remaining one million people and I urge the residents to turn up and register in order to benefit”, he added. Barasa said Kakamega County is still owed Sh293 Million pending bills from SHA, Sh72 Million being for level two and threes, 55 Million for level fours and Sh166 million for level Kakamega County Teaching and Referral Hospital, which is level 5. The governor confirmed that SHA will pay the county Sh100 million, being part of the reimbursement of the pending bills for Kakamega County and Teaching Referral hospital in the next two weeks. “We are still awaiting an analysis of 15 level four public health facilities and level two hospitals,” he added. Present were the Principal Secretary Medical Services Dr. Ouma Oluga and the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of SHA Dr. Mercy Mwangangi among others.

Uasin Gishu launches football tournament to nurture youth talent. Uasin Gishu Governor Jonathan Bii has called for increased investment in grassroots sports, saying nurturing young talent is essential in combating drug and substance abuse among youth while creating opportunities for economic empowerment. Speaking on Saturday during the launch of the Governor Chelilim Men’s Football Tournament at Naiberi Primary School grounds in Ainabkoi Sub-County, Bii said sporting activities provide young people with a positive platform to develop their abilities and remain focused on productive ventures. The governor noted that many young people risk falling into alcohol, marijuana and other forms of drug abuse when they lack meaningful activities to engage in. “Sports play a very important role in keeping our young people away from drugs and substance abuse. Without sports, many would have fallen into alcohol, marijuana and other narcotic drugs. We must protect our bodies and our minds because there is no spare body, and we must not allow our youth to destroy their future,” Bii said. He said Uasin Gishu, popularly known as the “County of Champions”, has a responsibility to strengthen sports development by investing in structures that identify and support emerging talent. Bii directed County Executive Committee Member for Sports Robert Kemei to lead efforts in training coaches and team managers across the county, saying qualified technical personnel are critical in developing competitive players. “We need trained coaches for every team, and we also need to train team managers. Once they are trained, we will register them and support them with a modest allowance so they can continue nurturing talent across the county,” he said. The governor said his administration would continue implementing programmes aimed at improving residents’ livelihoods despite political criticism. He cited the employment of Early Childhood Development Education (ECDE) teachers on permanent and pensionable terms and support for coffee farmers as some of the initiatives undertaken to improve household incomes. “Our focus is on delivering services to the people. We have employed ECDE teachers on permanent and pensionable terms, we are supporting our farmers to grow coffee and improve their incomes, and we will continue implementing programmes that transform the lives of our people,” Bii said. The Governor Chelilim Men’s Football Tournament has attracted more than 600 teams from across Uasin Gishu County and is expected to provide a competitive platform for young players to showcase their skills. The tournament will be played at ward, sub-county and county levels, with participating teams competing for a total prize purse of Sh14.1 million. Ward champions will receive Sh100,000, sub-county winners will take home Sh500,000, while the overall county champions will receive Sh1 million. Other top-performing teams will also receive cash awards. The launch featured an exhibition match between Huruma FC and Naiberi FC, with Huruma FC securing a 1-0 victory in a tightly contested encounter. The match attracted an enthusiastic crowd that witnessed players display skill, determination and teamwork, setting the pace for the tournament’s competitive fixtures. By Fredrick Maritim

Marsabit khat women traders receive Sh13.5 million business boost. Khat (miraa) women traders in Marsabit County have received a Sh13.5 million financial boost to expand their businesses and access affordable credit through a cooperative society. The funds were raised during a fundraiser presided over by Marsabit Governor Mohamud Ali at Marsabit Stadium, where he urged the beneficiaries to embrace financial discipline and use the resources responsibly to grow their enterprises. The traders said the funds will be managed through the Gumi Miraa Sacco and issued as loans to members to strengthen miraa businesses and improve their livelihoods. Governor Ali encouraged women traders to join and actively participate in cooperative societies, saying collective action was key to empowering communities and promoting economic growth. “When people come together, they are able to spur economic development. Kenya cannot develop through rhetoric and politics alone,” the governor said. He also called on political leaders to lower political temperatures by promoting peace and competing through ideas and development rather than tribal divisions. Ali thanked President William Ruto for promoting national unity, saying residents of Marsabit had resolved to support the government’s development agenda. He said marginalized communities had benefited from improved access to government services, including streamlined issuance of national identity cards after the removal of previous vetting requirements that hindered many residents from acquiring the documents. Marsabit Deputy Governor Solomon Riwe urged the women to remain united, noting that cooperative societies provide members with opportunities to access financial support and expand their businesses. He encouraged the traders to avoid divisions and work together to achieve economic empowerment. Petroleum Principal Secretary Kello Harsama called for stronger cooperative movements, saying organized groups were better positioned to attract support from the government and other development partners compared to individuals. Harsama urged the Department of Cooperatives to provide financial management training to members and advised the beneficiaries to invest the funds wisely to ensure sustainable business growth. Marsabit Woman Representative Naomi Waqo challenged the traders to diversify their businesses by exploring other opportunities such as clothing enterprises and grocery shops to increase their income sources. Gumi Miraa Sacco Chairlady Amina Dida said the cooperative has 350 members comprising miraa traders and farmers. She said the funds would be provided to members as affordable business loans, enabling them to expand their small-scale enterprises. Dida noted that many members had previously struggled to access loans due to lack of collateral but the new support had created an opportunity for them to grow their businesses. “These funds will enable my members who lacked collateral to borrow from Saccos to boost their businesses,” she said. The fundraiser attracted contributions from various leaders and institutions, with Governor Ali donating Sh4 million, including Sh2 million from county government staff. Cooperatives Cabinet Secretary Wycliffe Oparanya contributed Sh1 million, while Woman Representative Naomi Waqo and PS Kello Harsama donated Sh200,000 each. The beneficiaries expressed optimism that the financial support would improve their businesses, increase household incomes and strengthen the role of women in Marsabit’s local economy. By Sebastian Miriti and Anthony Melly

Met department releases rainfall advisory as short rains subside. By S, KNA The Kenya Meteorological Department (KMD) has advised Kenyans to brace for a drier day as the October-November –December short rains come to an end.
