Likuyani industrial park takes shape as Kakamega eyes industrial growth. The construction of Kakamega County Aggregation and Industrial Park (CAIP) in Likuyani Sub-County is gathering pace, with county officials expressing confidence that the project will unlock investment, create jobs and boost value addition for agricultural produce. The industrial park, a partnership between the National Government and the County Government of Kakamega, is expected to drive agro-processing and manufacturing, providing farmers with a ready market while strengthening the county’s industrial base. County Chief Officer for Public Works Pascal Omukanda during an inspection tour of the project with a team of technical officers to assess the progress of construction and ensure implementation expressed satisfaction with the progress made and directed the contractor to complete the works within the agreed timelines. “Timely completion of this project is critical. Any unnecessary delays will increase costs and place an additional financial burden on the county government,” he said. The Chief Officer noted that the industrial park is expected to generate hundreds of direct jobs in engineering, manufacturing, machine operation, administration and maintenance, while creating thousands of indirect opportunities in transport, logistics, packaging, security, hospitality and other support services. Omukanda said the facility will also attract private investors in agro-processing and manufacturing, enabling farmers to earn better returns through value addition instead of selling raw agricultural produce. Governor Fernandes Barasa equally reaffirmed the county government’s commitment to delivering the project. Speaking during a church service and fundraiser at Ivugwi P.A.G. Church in Likuyani Ward on Sunday, the Governor described the industrial park as a transformative investment that will spur economic growth and position Kakamega as a leading manufacturing hub in western Kenya. Barasa said the facility is expected to create close to 1,000 jobs once operational by attracting investors in agro-processing and other manufacturing industries, while offering local farmers a reliable market for value-added products. He said the county government is working closely with the National Government to ensure the project is completed on schedule so that residents can begin benefiting from the investment. Once operational, the industrial park will accommodate agro-processing plants, warehouses, cold storage facilities and packaging units, helping reduce post-harvest losses, enhance product quality and improve the competitiveness of Kakamega’s agricultural produce. Residents of Likuyani have welcomed the project, expressing hope that it will stimulate local businesses, create employment opportunities for young people and accelerate economic development across the sub-county. The County Aggregation and Industrial Park programme is a flagship national initiative aimed at promoting manufacturing, attracting private investment and accelerating industrialisation across Kenya, with the Likuyani facility expected to play a key role in transforming the economy of Kakamega County. By Linet Wafula

Governor Lusaka defends government’s development record. Bungoma Governor Kenneth Lusaka has mounted a spirited defence of President William Ruto’s development record, urging professionals in the county to take the lead in communicating the government’s achievements as the country heads towards the 2027 General Election. Speaking during the Bungoma Professionals Forum at Kibabii University on Saturday, Lusaka said professionals were best placed to objectively assess the government’s performance based on projects implemented over the past four years rather than political rhetoric. Lusaka said his interactions with the national government over the last four years had given him first-hand knowledge of the progress made in implementing development programmes in Bungoma and the wider Western region. “I have worked closely with this administration in negotiating for Bungoma’s development priorities, and I have seen project after project move from the drawing board to implementation,” he said. The governor said reforms in the sugar industry had begun reversing years of decline by settling historical debts owed to farmers, restructuring sugar factories and attracting private investment. He cited the revival of Nzoia Sugar Company as one of the government’s notable achievements, saying the factory was operating more efficiently following the installation of a new milling machine. “I visited Nzoia Sugar recently and the new milling machine promised by the President is fully operational. The challenge today is no longer low production but finding markets for more than 250,000 bags of sugar currently in storage,” he said. He said the fertiliser subsidy programme had enabled farmers to access inputs directly, eliminating middlemen who had long exploited growers, while coffee and tea farmers were now receiving better returns through direct payments. The governor also outlined major national government projects currently underway in Bungoma, saying they were laying the foundation for long-term economic growth. He said procurement for the expansion of Matulo Airstrip, including construction of a new passenger terminal and extension of the runway, had been completed and the contract would be awarded next week before construction begins. Lusaka further highlighted the construction of modern markets in Chwele, Sirisia, Mbakalo, Matisi and Lwandanyi, saying the facilities would provide improved trading spaces for farmers and small-scale traders. He said work was progressing on key roads, including the Musikoma-Sango-Napakhalo Road and the Turbo-Ekero-Ndalu Road, while the Kimilili-Kamukuywa Road project was set to commence after the award of the construction tender. Other flagship projects, he said, include the Kanduyi Smart City, the Affordable Housing Programme, rural electrification, the implementation of the Social Health Authority (SHA), the upgrade of Masinde Muliro Stadium and the proposed Standard Gauge Railway route through Bungoma. While acknowledging that some projects were still under construction, Lusaka maintained that implementation was on course. “I will not claim that every project is complete, but I can confidently say contractors are on site, procurement has been concluded and implementation is progressing satisfactorily,” he said. The governor also praised the national government’s improved disbursement of funds to counties, saying devolved units had for the first time ended the financial year with all their allocations fully released. “We closed the financial year with all the money due to counties already in our accounts. That has never happened before because counties were previously forced to wait for months for disbursements,” he said. Lusaka acknowledged that the Kenya Kwanza administration assumed office amid rising public debt, prolonged drought and global economic shocks but argued that it had sustained investment in infrastructure, agriculture, healthcare and social services despite the challenges. He challenged professionals to use their expertise and influence to explain government programmes to the public and counter misinformation. “The projects are visible and are transforming lives. President Ruto deserves another term to complete the programmes already underway,” Lusaka said. Speaking at the same forum, Industry Principal Secretary Dr. Juma Mukhwana said no administration since Independence had invested in Bungoma and the wider Western region as heavily as President Ruto’s government. He said the President had also appointed more leaders from Bungoma and the Western region to senior positions in government than previous administrations, demonstrating his commitment to inclusive leadership. “The projects being rolled out by the government are impactful and will significantly spur economic growth in this region. Professionals should take stock of these developments and help inform the electorate about what has been achieved,” said Mukhwana. Mining Principal Secretary Harry Kimtai urged professionals to support the government’s development agenda by helping dispel misinformation and ensuring residents receive accurate information on ongoing projects and programmes. “Professionals have a responsibility to demystify facts and counter misinformation so that wananchi understand exactly what the government is doing,” Kimtai said. Public Service Principal Secretary Dr. Jane Imbunya said the government had ensured development opportunities were distributed equitably across the country regardless of region. She said the government was also strengthening bilateral relations with other countries to create employment opportunities for Kenyan youth through labour mobility programmes. “The government has secured opportunities including scholarships, fellowships and overseas jobs targeting professionals and young people. I urge eligible Kenyans to take advantage of these opportunities by applying,” she said. Tourism Principal Secretary Prof Julius Bitok said every region had benefited from national government projects since President Ruto assumed office. “When I served as Immigration Principal Secretary, I facilitated the establishment of a passport office in Bungoma. Now, at the Ministry of Tourism, we are exploring several projects that the government will invest in to unlock the county’s tourism potential,” he said. Bitok urged professionals to rally behind President Ruto’s re-election bid, saying continuity would ensure the completion of ongoing development projects and programmes across Bungoma and the country. By Chris Mahandara

Daycare initiative gives young mothers second chance at education. A daycare programme established at a vocational training centre in Mathioya Constituency, Murang’a County, is enabling young mothers to return to school by providing safe childcare services while they pursue skills training. The initiative, introduced by the 360 Climate Institute, is helping teenage mothers rebuild their lives after pregnancies interrupted their education, allowing them to balance motherhood and learning without compromising the wellbeing of their children. At the centre of the programme is the“Cha Mama” Daycare Baby Crèche, where trained caregivers look after infants and toddlers from morning until evening as their mothers attend classes. The arrangement allows learners to concentrate on their studies while remaining close enough to breastfeed and check on their children during breaks. The programme was established in response to the growing number of young women who wanted to resume education but lacked reliable childcare support. For many beneficiaries, the initiative has become a pathway to restoring confidence, acquiring employable skills and securing a better future for themselves and their children. Jane Njeri, a beneficiary from Nyandarua County, said the programme enabled her to continue pursuing a catering course after giving birth. She explained that she enrolled at the institution while pregnant and took maternity leave before returning to complete her training with the support of the daycare facility. “I first learnt about this school online, applied and joined to study catering. At the time I was pregnant,” she said. Njeri noted that balancing exclusive breastfeeding with coursework has not been easy but said the daycare has made it possible for her to continue learning without neglecting her child. She expressed gratitude to the institution for creating an environment that allows young mothers to pursue education while fulfilling their parental responsibilities. Another beneficiary, Jane Wanjiru, has progressed from being one of the programme’s first students to becoming a trainer at the institution. She described the initiative as a turning point that transformed what once seemed like the end of her education into an opportunity for personal and professional growth. “I am a trainer and a beneficiary of the daycare centre. I would not be able to work without the daycare because it helps me juggle work and motherhood,” she said. Wanjiru encouraged other young mothers who had abandoned education after becoming pregnant to take advantage of similar opportunities and work towards rebuilding their futures. The success of the programme has also been attributed to caregivers such as Nancy Gakii, who ensures children are well-fed, safe and cared for throughout the day. Her work enables mothers to attend lessons with confidence, knowing their children are receiving proper care in a secure environment. The initiative has received positive support from members of the local community, who say it is helping reduce the stigma often associated with teenage motherhood. Resident Susan Wangui said many parents are unable to care for their daughters’ children during the day because they also have to work to support their families. “We have girls who dropped out of school after getting pregnant and sometimes, as parents, we cannot help with childcare because we also have to work the whole day,” she said. Joseph Gikungu welcomed the programme, saying it restores hope to young mothers who would otherwise struggle to return to school. “Allowing young mothers to come to school with their children makes me happy because it gives them hope,” he said. According to the Chief Executive Officer of the 360 Climate Institute, Daniel Irungu, the initiative was launched in 2024 after the organisation identified a growing need among young mothers seeking vocational training. “We realised there was a gap in society when we saw many young mothers who wanted skills but had no one to take care of their young children,” he said. Irungu said early parenthood should not mark the end of a young woman’s education or career aspirations, adding that access to skills training can help young mothers achieve financial independence. The institute’s founder and Board Chairperson, Hannah Muriithi, said the idea was inspired by the determination shown by young mothers who wanted to learn but were held back by childcare responsibilities. “We created a safe space where babies can play, learn and remain secure while their mothers attend training or teach different skills,” she said. Muriithi appealed to development partners, well-wishers and other organisations to support the programme so that more young mothers can benefit from vocational education and childcare services. She said expanding the initiative would enable more girls who dropped out of school due to pregnancy to acquire practical skills, improve their livelihoods and become economically self-reliant. The programme has emerged as a model of how targeted support can help young mothers overcome barriers to education, demonstrating that with access to childcare, skills training and community support, they can successfully balance motherhood and learning while creating brighter futures for themselves and their children. By Purity Mugo

New mosque for Muslim community in Isebania-Kuria. Muslim leaders have described the grand opening of the new Jamia Mosque at Isebania town in Kuria West Sub County as an important milestone for the Migori Muslim community. Led by the Council of Governors Chair and Wajir Governor Ahmed Abdullahi, the leaders said that the mosque will play a wider role apart from being a worship centre. The mosque, located at the border between Kenya and Tanzania, will serve the Muslim community within the region and across the border. Abdullahi said that the 2010 Kenyan Constitution guarantees freedom of conscience, religion and belief, which has played an essential and integral part in ensuring various religions coexist. Migori Governor Ochilo Ayacko noted that his administration was committed to supporting all communities living in the county to realise development and unity. “Migori is a cosmopolitan county and coexisting among different communities is paramount for our shared endeavors, unity and prosperity,” he said. He, however, encouraged the Muslim community in the county to continue investing to create jobs and drive the socio-economic transformative agenda for the betterment of the Migori residents. Suna East Member of Parliament (MP) and Minority Leader in Parliament Junet Mohamed disclosed that the new mosque will foster unity, teach Islamic knowledge and bring the Muslim community closer. “I am glad to witness the opening of the new Jamia Mosque, Isebania, which is a great milestone for the Muslim community along the Isebania-Sirare border,” said Junet. Rashid Omar, a resident of the Isebania area, said that the new mosque will give the Muslim community an avenue to worship, as well as a symbol of togetherness for the Muslim community in the Kuria region. The event, which concluded with a fund drive for the new mosque, brought together Lafey Member of Parliament (MP) Abdirahman Mohamed, Migori Woman Representative Fatuma Mohamed, Migori Deputy Governor Joseph Mahiri, businessman Abdullahi Kalmoi, sheikhs, imams, Muslim scholars and other local leaders. By Makokha Khaoya

Health CS inspects Nephrology, Urology facilities. Health Cabinet Secretary (CS) Aden Duale has inspected the East Africa Centre of Excellence in Nephrology and Urology to assess its readiness ahead of the commencement of the first phase of operations. The Government-funded Sh6 billion facility is one of Kenya’s largest investments in specialized renal and urological care and once operational, will serve Kenya and the wider East African Community by providing advanced diagnosis, treatment and management of kidney and urological diseases, while strengthening research, innovation and postgraduate training. During the inspection, Duale toured the Centre’s modern facilities, including modular operating theatres, Intensive Care and High Dependency Units, advanced diagnostic laboratories, MRI and radiology services, a biorepository, an integrated command centre and a renal replacement therapy unit equipped with 30 dialysis machines, including dedicated pediatric dialysis services. While also reviewing the progress on operational readiness, the CS, following Cabinet approval establishing the institution, highlighted that the Ministry is finalizing recruitment, operational systems, budgets, and essential medical supplies to ensure the Centre is fully prepared to begin service delivery. “The Centre has already contributed to specialist training by supporting 444 healthcare professionals and facilitating 375 kidney transplants through Kenyatta National Hospital,” he stated. Further, Duale announced that the Centre is expected to significantly expand access to specialized kidney and urological services, reduce referrals abroad, and strengthen Kenya’s contribution to regional healthcare excellence under the East African Community. Meanwhile, the inspection reaffirmed the Government’s commitment to investing in specialized healthcare, research and a highly skilled workforce to improve health outcomes and advance Universal Health Coverage. The Cabinet Secretary was accompanied by Director-General for Health Dr. Patrick Amoth, Head of the Kenya Blood Transfusion and Transplant Services Dr. Martin Sirengo, the Ministry’s Head of Curative and Nursing Services Dr. Andrew Toro as well as the Ministry’s Project Management Dr. Hossan Ajuck. ByLilian Gichohi

Authorities assure of exam security in Baringo. Baringo County Commissioner (CC) Stephen Kutwa has said adequate measures have been put in place for the over 48,000 candidates sitting for this year’s National Examinations in the area. Speaking to KNA in his office Monday, Kutwa said they have dispatched about 3,200 officers to secure 1,605 examination centres for Kenya Primary School Education Assessment (KPSEA), Kenya Certificate of Primary Education (KCPE), and Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE). The CC said the recently commissioned National Police Reservist (NPR) shall provide additional security backup, especially for institutions within conflict-prone areas of Baringo South and North, to ensure that the examinations are conducted without any major hitches. “We have put in place the necessary measures to ensure examinations run smoothly, and we have put in place officers to patrol schools in volatile areas,” he said. Kutwa said they are not leaving anything to chance since armed criminals could use the exam period to create fear and despondency among the peace-loving communities. He urged members of the public residing in the volatile regions to swiftly report any suspicious activities by people who may not mean well to them. On her part, Baringo Central Deputy County Commissioner Monicah Ithatwa, while presiding over the opening of the examination container in Kabarnet town, noted that the process was smooth except for some light rains in the morning, which nearly hampered the transportation of examination papers to various centres within the sub-county. However, she said that they were able to dispatch the day-one papers of KCPE and KPSEA in good time and expressed optimism that the process would run smoothly for the entire week. By Benson Kelio and Joshua Kibet

Road upgrade to boost connectivity in Kikuyu Constituency. Residents of Kikuyu Constituency are set to benefit from improved transport and easier access to essential services following the commissioning of the upgrading of the Ngong (Kibiku)–Kangiria Road, a project expected to enhance connectivity and stimulate socio-economic development in the area. The road improvement programme covers the Gwa-Thiru–Munyeki–Riu Nderi–Kibiku Road as well as the Musa Gitau (Ha Chege)–Kibagua–Kangiria–Riu Nderi Road, which serve as key links for residents, farmers, traders and motorists traveling within the constituency. Speaking during the commissioning of the project, Kikuyu Member of Parliament, Kimani Ichung’wah, said the road upgrade demonstrates the government’s commitment to improving infrastructure that directly impacts the lives of people. “These roads are more than just infrastructure; they are lifelines that connect our communities, open up markets for farmers and businesses, improve access to schools and healthcare facilities, and make daily travel safer and more convenient,” said Ichung’wah. The legislator noted that the improved roads will reduce travel time, lower vehicle maintenance costs and facilitate the movement of agricultural produce to markets, thereby supporting local economic growth. He added that reliable road infrastructure plays a critical role in attracting investment and encouraging business expansion while improving access to public institutions and social amenities. Area residents welcomed the project, expressing optimism that the upgraded roads will address long-standing transport challenges, particularly during the rainy season when some sections become difficult to navigate. The roads are expected to ease movement between villages and neighboring trading centres, enabling farmers to transport produce more efficiently while enhancing access to schools, health facilities and other government services. The project forms part of ongoing efforts by the national government to strengthen road infrastructure across Kikuyu Constituency through the rehabilitation and upgrading of key access roads aimed at supporting economic activities and improving mobility. Ichung’wah reaffirmed his commitment to pursuing development projects that respond to the needs of residents, saying investment in infrastructure remains a priority in transforming livelihoods and creating opportunities for growth. He urged contractors to maintain high construction standards and complete the works within the stipulated timelines to ensure residents begin enjoying the full benefits of the upgraded roads at the earliest possible time frame. By Eugene Kahigu and Grace Naishoo

LSK Announces nationwide court boycott over judicial concerns. The Law Society of Kenya (LSK) has announced a nationwide boycott of court proceedings on Wednesday, July 22, 2026, citing concerns over judicial accountability, corruption, and alleged misconduct within the justice system. Speaking during an LSK meeting in Machakos, LSK President and Senior Counsel Charles Kanjama said the action is aimed at pushing for urgent reforms to strengthen accountability and improve the administration of justice. “We deem it necessary to undertake a boycott to emphasize the seriousness of concerns raised by members and to call for meaningful institutional interventions,” Kanjama said. The boycott will take two forms. The first will be a one-day nationwide boycott on July 22, during which advocates will refrain from participating in court hearings and applications. The second will involve an indefinite targeted boycott of specific courts presided over by judges and judicial officers who have obtained court orders preventing the Judicial Service Commission (JSC) or the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC) from processing corruption allegations against them. Kanjama said the success of the measures depends on the cooperation of advocates across the country. He noted that the LSK Council had held several engagements with the Chief Justice to address concerns raised by members but had not achieved the desired progress. The issues cited by the society include corruption, judicial misconduct, abuse of office, case backlogs, frequent adjournments, and delays in delivery of rulings and judgments. “Where sustainable engagement does not yield adequate progress, the Council has a statutory duty to take lawful action,” Kanjama said. He emphasized that while the LSK remains committed to protecting judicial independence, such independence must be accompanied by accountability, integrity, transparency, and responsiveness to concerns raised by court users. As part of its resolutions, the society plans to establish a structured and confidential mechanism through which advocates can report concerns relating to judicial performance, misconduct, registry challenges, and delays in court processes. Kanjama called on LSK branches countrywide to support the resolutions by creating awareness among members, collecting feedback, and coordinating local engagements. The society said it will continue pursuing dialogue with the Judiciary while proceeding with the planned boycott. By Anne Kangero

Government urges Tana River communities to surrender illegal firearms. The government has renewed calls on feuding communities in Tana River County to voluntarily surrender all illegally held firearms before the expiry of an ongoing amnesty period and the commencement of a planned disarmament operation. The Ministry of Interior issued a 60-day amnesty period more than a month ago, giving residents in the conflict-prone county an opportunity to surrender illicit weapons without facing arrest, interrogation or prosecution. The move is aimed at reducing the proliferation of illegal firearms and restoring peace in a region that has experienced recurring resource-based conflicts. Tana River has for years witnessed tensions between nomadic pastoralist communities and farming communities over access to scarce water sources, grazing land and agricultural resources. Security experts and local leaders have linked the recurring disputes to prolonged drought, climate change effects and increased pressure on natural resources, factors that have intensified competition between communities. Tana River County Commissioner Joseph Mwangi has urged residents in possession of illegal firearms to take advantage of the amnesty period and hand over the weapons to security agencies. Mwangi, who chairs the County Security and Intelligence Committee (CSIC), said the voluntary surrender initiative provides an opportunity for individuals holding unlicensed firearms to avoid legal action once the amnesty period ends. “The gun amnesty is expected to reduce the volume of illegal firearms in circulation and by doing so, the government aims to enhance public safety and security,” he said. The administrator warned that individuals who fail to surrender illegal weapons and continue supporting the circulation of firearms would face the full force of the law after the amnesty period. He said the government would deploy National Police Reservists to various parts of the county after the disarmament exercise to strengthen security and protect lives and property. The renewed push for voluntary surrender follows a series of inter-community clashes reported in Tana North, Bangale and Galedyertu sub-counties, where six people were killed last month during conflicts linked to competition over water and pasture resources. Mwangi revealed that more than seven serviceable AK-47 rifles and associated ammunition had already been surrendered voluntarily during the ongoing exercise. He, however, said the number remained insignificant compared to the suspected number of illegal firearms still held by individuals and groups in the county. “We know the number of illegal arms and ammunition given up so far during the surrender period is insignificant compared to what we believe is still being hidden,” he said. He attributed the recoveries to continued engagement between communities and security agencies aimed at encouraging peaceful coexistence and reducing the circulation of illegal weapons. The County Commissioner called on residents to support government efforts by reporting individuals holding illegal firearms and encouraging them to surrender the weapons. He also urged youths involved in communal conflicts to disengage from violence and embrace peaceful solutions to disputes. Mwangi spoke in Bura Sub-County during the commissioning of a water project, where he was accompanied by Cabinet Secretary for East African Community (EAC), Arid and Semi-Arid Lands (ASALs), and Regional Development Beatrice Askul Moe. The Commissioner said security agencies had received information that approximately nine illegal firearms were being held by herders in Chwewele Ward, Bura Sub-County. “We have credible information that about nine illegal firearms are being held by herders in Chwewele Ward in Bura Sub-County, and we still urge all concerned to voluntarily submit these arms by next week,” Mwangi said. He warned that police and other security agencies would take action against individuals found in possession of illegal firearms and ammunition once the amnesty period expires. CS Moe also encouraged residents to surrender illicit weapons, saying the exercise was aimed at making the country safer for citizens and visitors. She said peace and security are shared responsibilities requiring cooperation between communities, government agencies and local leaders. Moe urged residents to avoid actions that fuel conflict and instead promote dialogue, unity and peaceful coexistence. “Let us all keep our peace and security intact because without peace and unity there would be no meaningful development,” she said. The government said the disarmament initiative is part of broader efforts to enhance security, prevent loss of lives and create an environment where development projects can thrive in Tana River County. By Hussein Abdullahi

Motorcycle riders to transport patients’ specimens under new referral system. Patients seeking laboratory services in Kuresoi North and Kuresoi South sub-counties will no longer be required to travel to referral hospitals after the Nakuru County Government introduced an Integrated Specimen Referral System (ISRS) that uses trained motorcycle riders to transport medical specimens. Under the new system, specimens collected at dispensaries and health centres will be transported safely to the nearest referral hospital with laboratory facilities, while test results will be transmitted electronically back to the originating health facility, enabling patients to receive treatment closer to their homes. County Executive Committee Member (CECM) for Health Care Services Roselyn Mungai said the initiative is aimed at improving access to diagnostic services, reducing patient travel costs and ensuring timely medical interventions. She said the County Health Department is strengthening its logistics network by restoring grounded motorcycles, training riders and streamlining fleet management to fully operationalise the Integrated Specimen Referral System. “Trained riders will transport patient specimens safely and securely, completely sparing vulnerable patients from travelling long distances to high-level facilities for basic laboratory tests. By strengthening local delivery systems and minimizing avoidable clinical errors, the County Government is ensuring that every citizen receives safe, timely and patient-centred healthcare,” said Ms Mungai. She spoke during a strategy meeting with regional health team leaders from Kuresoi North and Kuresoi South sub-counties convened to review implementation plans and strengthen service delivery. The CECM said riders enlisted under the programme will undergo refresher training before full implementation of the system. She noted that the referral model has already undergone a pilot phase, which demonstrated improved patient management, reduced turnaround time for laboratory results and lower transport costs for patients. According to Ms Mungai, the trained and equipped riders will transport sensitive medical specimens from dispensaries, health centres and community health units to sub-county and county referral laboratories for specialised testing. She added that licensed boda boda riders may also be engaged whenever additional transport capacity is required, with the county facilitating the service to ensure uninterrupted movement of specimens. The CECM described specimen referral as a critical component of an efficient healthcare system, saying timely transportation of samples enhances diagnosis and treatment while improving overall patient outcomes. She said the initiative will expand access to specialised laboratory services regardless of where patients seek treatment, ensuring that residents in remote areas benefit from the same quality of diagnostic services available in major hospitals. The Integrated Specimen Referral System is among several initiatives being implemented by Governor Susan Kihika’s administration to improve healthcare delivery across Nakuru County. Ms Mungai said the programme is also expected to strengthen disease surveillance, facilitate faster clinical decision-making and promote equitable access to healthcare by reducing travel burdens and out-of-pocket expenses for patients. “This is a sustainable intervention that should be integrated with Primary Health Care to strengthen Universal Health Coverage and ensure long-term improvements in healthcare delivery,” she said. Implementation activities will include dissemination of the ISRS work plan, training of sub-county coordinators, sensitisation of healthcare workers and periodic performance reviews in the pilot sub-counties before wider rollout. Beyond improving logistics, Ms Mungai said the county government is promoting a culture of accountability among healthcare workers by encouraging staff to identify and resolve operational challenges before they affect service delivery. She urged health officers to take ownership of their facilities and work collaboratively to sustain quality healthcare services. The CECM said the success of the Integrated Specimen Referral System will depend on innovation, teamwork and professionalism, adding that the reforms are intended to ensure quality healthcare remains accessible to all residents as a fundamental right rather than a privilege. By Jane Ngugi and Caroline Nyakio

Researchers identify solutions to reduce pesticide residues on farm produce. Did you know that the simple act of soaking your fresh leafy spinach in salty water, then washing them under running water before cooking them could be the difference between living longer or dying earlier? A report by the Kenya Organic Agriculture Network (KOAN), in partnership with the Route to Food Initiative (RTIFI) and the Heinrich Böll Foundation (HBF) has demonstrated that these rudimentary practices can reduce the average detectable pesticide residue by 72.4 %. The joint report titledPesticide Residues in Selected Vegetables from Kenyan markets and Effectiveness of Household Methods for Residue Reductionlists a total of eight simple home practices that have been found to effectively address the challenge of pesticide residues in foods commonly consumed by majority of Kenyans on a daily basis. During the study, four vegetable varieties namely bulb onions, kales, spinach and tomatoes were employed under the study. The 45 samples used in the study were sourced from various markets in Nairobi and Nakuru cities. The markets were selected since most of their fresh produce are sourced from upcountry farms in Nyeri, Nyandarua, Machakos, Kirinyaga and Kajiado counties. “On average, soaking(vegetables) in salty water, washing under running water plus cooking gave the highest average reduction at 72.4 %; this was followed by washing in running water plus blanching at 70 %, then soaking in baking soda water plus washing and cooking had 69.8 %, while soaking in baking soda, washing plus cooking had 69.8 % reduction. This was followed by vinegar at 64.6 %, washing under running water at an average reduction of 61 %, and lastly, a 56.6% reduction was achieved with soaking in baking soda plus washing under running water,” read the report released on July 19, 2026 at the Central Bank of Kenya Institute of Monetary Studies during a stakeholders’ forum dubbed Food Safety in Kenya:From Evidence to Action. From the study onions exhibited the best pesticide reduction rate with all seven treatment methods within a range of between 98.7% and 99.7%. Tomatoes came second with a high of 68.3 % residue reduction rate after being soaked in baking soda followed by washing under running water before cooking. Spinach came third at 65.5 % after soaking in salty water then washing under running water and later cooking. On the other hand, soaking kales in vinegar, washing them under running water and finally cooking them achieved a 62.3% reduction in residues. The report also revealed that 78 % of the samples tested during the study had detectable pesticides while a third had surpassed EU Maximum Residue Limits (MRLs). MRLs is the maximum concentration of a pesticide residue on food or feed of plant and animal origin that is legally tolerated. The pesticides detected above EU MRLs comprised fungicides, insecticides, an herbicide and a miticide, laying bare the diversity of pesticide products farmers employ in vegetable husbandry. Tomatoes carried the highest burden, accounting for two-thirds of the non-compliant samples while onions came relatively clear. The report also found that household preparation methods can reduce pesticide residues by 60 to 70 %. “Food safety is everyone’s responsibility. This dialogue brings together evidence, experience and diverse voices to identify practical actions that can strengthen Kenya’s food system, from the farm to the consumer’s table, alongside data on pesticide residue reduction levels,” said Eustace Kiare, KOAN Executive Director during the release of the findings at the In 2024, a baseline study in Nyeri, Meru, Kirinyaga, Taita Taveta and Makueni counties on kales, tomatoes and onions by the Pest Control Products Board (PCPB) showed that out of 105 samples, 33 (31 %) had pesticide residues exceeding the EU-MRLs. The report further noted that previous pesticide monitoring researches had demonstrated that a proportion of vegetables being consumed in the country contain pesticide that exceed internationally recognized MRLs. KOAN is therefore calling for routine surveillance of pesticides in order to provide scientific evidence for evaluating compliance with pesticide regulations, assessing consumer exposure and informing national food safety policies. “Such information is particularly relevant in settings where consumers rely primarily on domestic food preparation to minimize dietary exposure. The results are expected to benefit regulatory agencies, public health practitioners, agricultural extension services, researchers, development partners, and consumers by providing evidence that supports safer agricultural production and healthier food preparation practices,” the report explains. According to a 2024 joint report by PCPB and FAO, Kenya’s pesticide imports rose from 14,600 tons in 2015 to 19,932 metric tons by 2020, catalyzed by a growing agricultural production and market demand. Another report in 2022 showed that 76 % of the total volume of pesticides used in Kenya contained or more active ingredients that are labelled as Highly Hazardous Pesticides (HHPs). Both WHO and FAO identify HHPs in pesticides based on their toxicity to human health, persistence in the environment and toxicity to aquatic life and pollinators. The report therefore insists that though the samples from the study exhibited pesticide residue below regulatory limits, excessive or repeated dietary exposure to certain pesticides has in the past been associated with adverse health outcomes. “Acute exposure (to pesticides) may cause symptoms such as nausea, dizziness, skin irritation, and respiratory distress, whereas long-term exposure has been linked to neurological disorders, endocrine disruption, reproductive impairment, developmental abnormalities and increased risks of cancers,” reads the findings. “Consequently, routine surveillance of pesticide residues remains an important component of national food safety systems.” Dr Harun Warui, RTFI programme Coordinator says Kenya lacks a single fix to address the challenge of harmful pesticides on human food and requires all stakeholders on board to find a way around the problem. Dr Warui argued that Kenya should not rely on policies in order to cut down on use of pesticides but should instead come up with less hazardous pest control practices that do not imperil both man and environment. “Today’s launch offers households a practical way to cut down pesticide exposure, but it cannot stand alone as the fix. The evidence keeps pointing in the same direction: without stronger regulation, unsafe food linked to highly hazardous pesticides will keep reaching consumers,” said Dr Warui. “We need a 360-degree approach, one that pairs household action with firmer enforcement of pesticide standards, so that safety does not depend on what happens in the kitchen alone. Agroecology gives us a further route to the same goal, growing food in ways that reduce our reliance on hazardous pesticides in the first place, rather than only managing their residues after the fact.” Dr Johnson Nduhiu Gitahi, a staff at the Nairobi University Department of Public Health, Pharmacology and Toxicology explained the need of the entire study was to explore practical solutions to safer foods in Kenya. Dr Gitahi said all those involved in the entire food chain must make sure what is grown in the farms is safe for the kitchen before it finds its way to the dining table. “Our goal was to provide evidence that people can use every day. Safer food starts on the farm, but simple steps at home can also help reduce pesticide residues before vegetables are eaten,” he stated. Early this year eight non-governmental organizations drawn from East Africa had called for concrete policies to help safeguard both man and environment from effects of HHPs. In a joint statement released on March 27 this year, the group under the umbrella of East Africa Pesticide Network had noted the steps the region had taken in reducing the usage of hazardous pesticides but warned findings showed there was still presence of HHPs in the ecosystem. The network had brought together Greenpeace Africa, RTFI, Food Safety Coalition Uganda, Global Consumer Center, Broederlijk Delen, SEATINI, Tanzania Organic Agricultural Movement and Premium Kenya. The report followed findings that were presented during the East Africa Pesticides, Environment and Health Interdisciplinary Symposium held in Kisumu from November 5 to 6 2025. The group wanted the region to come up with strong enforcement, transparent registration processes, and regular monitoring and publication of data on pesticide reduction. In addition, they wanted governments from the East Africa region to develop an effective surveillance of acute and chronic pesticide poisoning and coordinated regional action to prevent cross-border pesticide trade in hazardous products. “At the policy level, we recognize that important regulatory steps are already being taken to protect our health and the environment, as well as transboundary control of hazardous products. In June 2025, Kenya announced the withdrawal of 77 per cent of products and restrictions on an additional 202. Earlier this year, Tanzania announced the phase-out of 805 products, a step that demonstrates the growing recognition of pesticide risks. These actions signal growing recognition of the risks posed by pesticides; however, regulatory bans alone are not enough.” read the statement. According to the report, global pesticide uses in East Africa rose from 1.8 million tons to 3.7 million tons between 1990 and 2022, posing a challenge in tackling entry of harmful chemicals into the region. On the other hand, pesticide imports into Africa increased 5.7 times between 2002 and 2022, a pointer to broader agricultural intensification trends driven by changing climatic patterns, pest pressure and food production demands. During the same period, pesticide used on food crops exceeded the allowed safety limits posing health risks to both humans and the environment. “Today, we present findings of studies shared at the symposium that found pesticide residues in drinking water sources, agricultural soils, fresh produce, and ambient air in parts of East Africa. These effects are as a result of exposure, use and misuse of pesticides products that have already been banned in their countries of origin, but are available and sold in countries in the global south, such as Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania,” continued the report. “In some food samples, pesticide limits exceeded established maximum residual levels (MRLs). Health research also documented cases of acute pesticide poisoning and identified links between occupational pesticide exposure and neurological, mental health, and reproductive outcomes among agricultural workers.” To cut down on use of HHPs in the region, respective governments were advised to among other things adhere to existing international agreements such as the Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm conventions which outline regulations on hazardous waste movement and trade. At the regional level, member states were urged to adhere to EAC Guidelines on Data Requirements for the Registration of Conventional Chemical Pesticides Used in Agriculture and Forestry adopted during the 38thExtra –Ordinary Council of Ministers on January 30 2019. The Convection provided applicants with better information on the data and studies on how they should submit to national pesticide registration. “Despite the legal frameworks, there are existential challenges to implementation, corporate control over the food system, and weak negotiation capacity between the EAC and the global north. These have continued to influence the continuous trade in and use of highly hazardous pesticides in the region. East African countries still struggle to coordinate joint actions on the regulation and control of the trade in and use of highly hazardous pesticides. There are still challenges of porous borders where pesticides registered, traded, or used in one country often move across borders through formal and informal markets,” highlighted the report. The East Africa Pesticide Network also called for continuous adoption of viable alternatives such as crop diversification, use of biological control agents, soil health management, habitat management for natural enemies and farmer-led integrated pest management. The group noted that such a paradigm shift has in the past helped reduce chemical dependence while safeguarding the soil ecosystem. The network also called for stronger regional collaborative action involving the governments, farmers, researchers, civil societies among others in pushing for initiatives that will protect the public health, food chain and the environment through adopting safer agricultural production practices. In October 2023 KOAN), Biodiversity and Biosafety Association of Kenya(biba), and RTFI had called stakeholders in the agricultural sector to come up with an effective panacea on the use of HHPs in the country. The trio, while admitting the then efforts which were being undertaken towards protecting the safety of crops in regard to the use of pesticides in the country had argued that such efforts should bring more players on board. “A collaborative effort among regulatory bodies, farmers, environmentalists and civil society is crucial to finding a balanced and sustainable approach to pesticide use, especially concerning the use of Highly Hazardous Pesticides in Kenya,” read a joint press statement from the group. “We agree that the responsible use and handling of pesticides are essential. However, we must acknowledge that the responsibility for safe pesticide use is beyond the farmers’ ability. Required mitigation measures like buffer zones to safeguard communities or water resources often can’t be implemented. Beyond the responsibility of the farmer, pesticide companies should also play an essential role in ensuring the safe use, disposal and handling of their products through extended producer responsibility (EPR).” In September 13 2022, RTFI released a report detailing how the majority of Kenyans could be consuming foods laced with HHPs posing a threat to their overall wellbeing. The reportToxic Business; Highly Hazardous Pesticides in Kenya,identified maize, wheat, coffee, potatoes, kales and tomatoes as consumers of the largest volumes of pesticides heavily laced with HHPs. As a result, the crops which form the bulk of the country’s food sources were said to be exposed to a range of toxic substances, a threat to both consumers and the environment. Further, according to the 40-page report, only six out of 310 pesticides in use in the country at the time could be qualified as bio pesticides (derived from natural materials such as plant and animal products and therefore considered safe), accounting for a paltry 2 per cent of the total pesticide volume. “Common food items in Kenya households such as maize, wheat, coffee, potatoes, kales and tomatoes require the largest volumes of pesticides, with a heavy reliance on HHPs.These crops are exposed to a range of toxic substances, posing significant threats to both consumers and the environment,” read the report’s findings. “Only six out of the 310 pesticide products used in Kenya are bio pesticides, accounting for a mere 2 per cent of the total pesticide volume. Meanwhile, Highly Hazardous Pesticides account for a shocking 76 per cent of the total volume used. This huge disparity indicates the urgent need to promote bio pesticides.”. But responding to the report later, PBCB and aak/GROW Fresh Produce Consortium of Kenya (FPC Kenya) faulted the findings insisting the State had been keen in ensuring pesticides landing in the country do not impair the health of man, beast and environment. The board also clarified that only insecticides that meet the required MRLs were allowed into the country. “Ensuring consumer and pesticide user safety is our top priority. Food safety is key during approval of pesticides that is why Maximum Residue Levels are required,” said PCPB then acting CEO Fredrick Muchiri. “The Route to Food initiative report is not factual. Ban means total ban on manufacture and use. You cannot ban a pesticide and continue producing for other people,” he said. The official similarly defended the use of pesticides in the country saying they do play a crucial role in safeguarding crop production by combating pests and disease-causing agents But KOAN, RTFI and biba claimed there was a need to follow a hazard assessment for registering very toxic pesticides (WHO 1a, WHO 1b, and so-called CMR (carcinogenic, mutagenic and reproduction toxic pesticides)) as a matter of urgency. The NGOs said such hazard assessments should focus on the inherent properties of pesticides, regardless of their use patterns. “It is essential to strike a balance between risk and hazard assessments to ensure comprehensive safety, as many of the Highly Hazardous Pesticides (HHP) mentioned in the recently launched report Toxic Business: Highly Hazardous Pesticides in Kenya are very toxic, for example, beta-cyfluthrin. We agree that the responsible use and handling of pesticides are essential.” they pointed out. And in response to PCPB’s stance on importation of pesticides currently flagged in Europe, the NGOs had remarked that the products under question had been outlawed due to their health risk to both humans and the environment. They therefore called for exploration of friendlier means of food production that rely less on agrochemicals and also guarantee bumper harvests and access to safe food for the country. “We encourage PCPB to explore sustainable pest management alternatives that prioritize both crop protection and the long-term health of Kenyan farmers and consumers, and the environment. We would like to emphasize that most of the pesticides that are banned in Europe are withdrawn from the market because of their unacceptable risk towards the environment and human health and not because of less pest pressure.” They stressed. “We would also like to emphasize that a system change of agricultural production is necessary and not just a substitution from one pesticide to the other, to achieve safe food in an enabling environment.” Among pesticides ingredients considered highly toxic and commonly used by farmers in the country by then included chlorpyrifos, acetochlor, glyphosate, 2,4-D, mancozeb and chlorothalonil. Active ingredients, such as bifenthrin, dichlorvos, diazinon, carbaryl, fipronil, Thiamethoxam, and carbendazim, have already been outlawed in Europe. By Samuel Maina

Government launches Sh34 billion programme to strengthen climate resilience. The Government has officially launched the Integrated Natural Resources Management Programme (INReMP), a Sh34.1 billion (USD 262 million) initiative that will run for eight years to strengthen climate resilience, restore degraded ecosystems, improve food security and enhance livelihoods for more than two million Kenyans. The programme, jointly funded by the Government of Kenya and the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD), targets 407,176 households across 10 counties in western Kenya through investments in climate-smart agriculture, natural resource conservation and sustainable rural development. Prime Cabinet Secretary and Cabinet Secretary for Foreign and Diaspora Affairs Musalia Mudavadi presided over the national launch at the University of Eldoret under the theme,“Building Climate Resilient Livelihoods Through Inclusive and Sustainable Development.” Mudavadi described the programme as a major milestone in the country’s efforts to address climate change while accelerating socio-economic transformation through sustainable management of natural resources. He said the initiative would enable counties endowed with rich agricultural potential, biodiversity and water resources to better respond to the growing challenges of climate change, environmental degradation, food insecurity and rural poverty. “Implementing this programme demonstrates our determination as a nation to turn these challenges into opportunities by restoring our environment, improving livelihoods and strengthening our resilience. It will contribute to our socio-economic transformation journey and secure a better future for present and future generations,” Mudavadi said. The Prime Cabinet Secretary was accompanied by Environment, Climate Change and Forestry Cabinet Secretary Dr. Deborah Mlongo Barasa, Agriculture Principal Secretary Dr. Paul Ronoh, Environment Principal Secretary Dr. Eng. Festus Ngeno, Treasury Principal Secretary Dr. Chris Kiptoo, Gender Principal Secretary Anne Wang’ombe, Trade Principal Secretary Regina Ombam, Uasin Gishu Governor Jonathan Bii Chelilim and other senior national and county government officials. The programme will be implemented in Elgeyo Marakwet, West Pokot, Trans Nzoia, Uasin Gishu, Nandi, Kakamega, Kericho, Kisumu, Homa Bay and Migori counties, which continue to experience increasing climate-related shocks affecting agriculture, water resources and livelihoods. According to Mudavadi, the focus on western Kenya reflects the urgent need to address environmental degradation and strengthen resilience in one of the country’s most productive agricultural regions. He noted that Kenya is richly endowed with forests, wetlands, rivers, fertile agricultural land and other natural resources that form the backbone of food production, water security, biodiversity conservation and the rural economy. However, he observed that these resources continue to face mounting pressure from land degradation, deforestation, declining soil fertility, biodiversity loss and shrinking water catchments, all of which threaten sustainable development. Mudavadi said INReMP provides a comprehensive response to these challenges by integrating environmental conservation with livelihood improvement and institutional capacity building. The programme is anchored on three strategic pillars. The first focuses on ecosystem services and climate action through restoration and protection of forests, wetlands, watersheds and critical water towers, particularly the Mau and Cherangany ecosystems. The second pillar seeks to improve sustainable rural livelihoods by promoting regenerative agriculture, climate-smart farming technologies, irrigation, value addition, enterprise development and commercialization of nature-based value chains to increase household incomes. The third pillar focuses on strengthening institutions by supporting policy development, enhancing coordination among implementing agencies and establishing regional offices to oversee programme implementation. Mudavadi said the programme’s overall goal is to improve food, nutrition and income security for rural households while ensuring communities live within sustainable and climate-resilient ecosystems. He added that the initiative seeks to enhance integrated natural resource management while increasing resilience to climate change, particularly among women, youth, persons with disabilities, indigenous communities and other vulnerable groups. The Prime Cabinet Secretary said restoration of degraded landscapes will involve supporting communities to conserve forests, rangelands, wetlands, water sources and agricultural land through soil and water conservation, carbon sequestration and climate action initiatives. He said the programme would also improve agricultural productivity by promoting modern farming technologies, climate-smart agriculture, irrigation infrastructure, value chain development and rural enterprise growth to create employment and increase household incomes. Mudavadi called for greater investment in capacity building for national and county governments, community institutions and local organisations to ensure successful implementation of the programme under the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda. He noted that deliberate inclusion of women, youth and vulnerable groups would ensure equitable access to opportunities created by the programme while stimulating entrepreneurship, job creation and social inclusion in rural areas. “The successful implementation of INReMP will strengthen our national food system. Building on lessons from previous natural resource management programmes will improve productivity, reduce vulnerability, strengthen food and nutrition security and create more resilient communities,” he said. Mudavadi underscored the importance of partnerships, accountability and community ownership, saying the programme’s success would depend on close collaboration between the national government, county governments, development partners, technical experts and local communities. He urged county governments to integrate the programme into their development plans, provide effective leadership and coordinate implementation to maximise impact. The Prime Cabinet Secretary also challenged communities to actively participate in planning, protect investments made under the programme and strengthen local institutions to ensure long-term sustainability. He said success would ultimately be measured by restored ecosystems, improved household incomes, increased agricultural productivity, empowered women and youth, strengthened community institutions and healthier rural environments. Mudavadi expressed confidence that successful implementation would encourage IFAD and other development partners to continue supporting Kenya’s green growth agenda and environmental restoration efforts. He said the initiative aligns with the country’s broader climate action commitments and sustainable development goals by restoring degraded landscapes, protecting water resources, strengthening food systems and improving livelihoods. Calling on leaders and residents of the beneficiary counties to fully embrace the programme, Mudavadi said it provides an opportunity to transform rural economies while safeguarding natural resources for future generations. “Let us use this programme to restore landscapes, protect water resources, improve farming systems, strengthen rural enterprises and build hope for beneficiary communities. Through ownership, participation and accountability, we can secure lasting benefits for all,” he said. By Ekuwam Sylvester and Nelson Obwana

Community Health Committees trained. At least forty-eight members of Community Health Committees (CHCs) in Kajiado North have completed a five-day training programme aimed at improving public health surveillance at the grassroots. The training, organized by the Ministry of Health in partnership with CFK Africa, equipped participants with skills in leadership, governance, conflict resolution, resource mobilization, communication, advocacy and community health oversight. The newly trained CHCs were drawn from Kware A, Mayor Road, Scheme 6, Olekasasi B, Lemelepo, Oloosurutia, Gichagi and Olepolos community health units. They join another 60 committee members trained during the first phase of the programme earlier this year. Speaking during the closing ceremony in Ngong, Kajiado North Sub-County Community Health Strategy Coordinator and Health Promotion Officer Susan Nesenke expressed confidence that the trainees would apply the knowledge gained to improve healthcare delivery in their communities. “I expect the Community Health Committees to implement what they have learned by providing effective oversight to community health promoters and advocating for improved health services. This will strengthen the link between communities and health facilities,” she said. Kajiado North Sub-County Medical Officer of Health Dr. Marion Mukira said the committees would play a critical role in supervising Community Health Promoters (CHPs) and supporting efforts to build healthier communities. She commended CFK Africa for partnering with the Ministry of Health to strengthen community health systems across Kajiado County. CFK Africa Programme Officer for Event-Based Surveillance Dorine Ochieng said the training was designed to enhance disease surveillance and early detection of public health threats at the community level. “The committees are important because they work closely with Community Health Promoters and residents. Many of the members are village elders who can quickly identify and report unusual health events, enabling timely public health response,” said Ochieng. She noted that following the first phase of the training, the sub-county had recorded improved reporting of health events by Community Health Promoters, attributing the progress to stronger collaboration between CHCs and CHPs. Kajiado County Chief Officer for Public Health and Sanitation Eddy Kimani said community health committees and community health promoters remain the foundation of preventive and promotive healthcare because of their close interaction with residents. Kimani pledged the county government’s support to the newly trained committees, including issuing them with certificates and identification badges to facilitate their work in the communities. “With the establishment of more community health units, we expect improved health indicators, which are critical for planning and budget allocation,” he said. He also lauded the 167 community health promoters serving Kajiado North for their commitment and reaffirmed the county government’s commitment, under Governor Joseph Ole Lenku, to continue supporting them through the payment of stipends. The community health committees will serve as the link between communities and health facilities, overseeing the work of community health promoters while helping ensure residents access quality healthcare services. By Peter Muteti

Teso farmers urged to preserve maize for food security. Farmers in Teso North have been urged to preserve adequate stocks of their newly harvested maize for household consumption before selling any surplus produce. Local leaders said maintaining sufficient food reserves until the next planting and harvesting season is essential in safeguarding household food security and protecting families from possible shortages. The advice follows reports that some farmers have started selling freshly harvested maize at between Sh50 and Sh60 per gorogoro (two-kilogram tin), despite the same quantity retailing at about Sh100 at Malaba Market. Teso North Member of Parliament Oku Kaunya, who led the appeal, expressed concern that selling maize at low prices could force farmers to dispose of much of their harvest without gaining meaningful returns. He warned that such decisions could leave households with inadequate food reserves and limited income after months of farming efforts. Kaunya said reports of declining maize production in some parts of the country should encourage farmers to prioritize food storage before marketing their surplus. He also urged farmers to diversify into other crops such as cassava and groundnuts to strengthen household resilience, improve nutrition, and create alternative income sources during seasons of poor maize performance. The concerns come as various counties undertake assessments to establish maize production levels following changing weather patterns. In Uasin Gishu County, the county government, in collaboration with the Ministry of Agriculture, has started a countywide digital maize crop assessment after indicating that approximately 30 per cent of the crop had been affected by several weeks of dry conditions. According to the county government, the exercise aims to determine the extent of crop damage and generate information to guide interventions and policy decisions. In Busia County, the Department of Agriculture is also conducting a two-week Rapid Maize Performance Assessment of the 2026 long-rains maize crop to evaluate crop performance, estimate expected production, and support agricultural planning and food security interventions. The assessment, which began on July 13, 2026, involves agricultural officers and agripreneurs visiting farms across the county to collect crop performance data. Teso North Deputy County Commissioner Solomon Kitai and Kenya National Union of Teachers (KNUT) Teso Branch Chairman Alex Omoit supported the call for farmers to make careful decisions when selling their produce. Teso North Agricultural Officer Gertrude Wambia advised farmers against selling maize individually, saying they risk receiving low prices due to weak bargaining power. She encouraged farmers to market their produce collectively through Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs), Common Interest Groups (CIGs), and cooperative societies to negotiate better prices and access reliable markets. “I urge all farmers to work closely with agripreneurs who provide training, link them to service providers, and connect them with buyers through FPOs. When you harvest your produce, please do not rush to sell individually. Let agripreneurs help you secure better prices,” Wambia said during a recent farmers’ field day in Amagoro. The leaders emphasized that proper post-harvest management, collective marketing, and crop diversification would enable farmers to protect their livelihoods and improve returns from agriculture. By Moses Wekesa

Over 20 teams set for action-packed Prinsloo Sevens Championship. More than 20 teams are set to battle for honours during the 17th edition of the National 7s Prinsloo Sevens Championships scheduled for Nakuru Athletics Club (NAC) next weekend. The tournament, which returns to Nakuru for the 13th time, will mark the opening leg of the 2026 SportPesa National Sevens Circuit, with rugby fans expected to witness high-intensity action from some of the country’s leading clubs. The 2026 Prinsloo Sevens will officially kick off on July 25 and 26, 2026, at the NAC as teams begin their campaign for national circuit glory. Tournament Director Edward Moseti said preparations are complete and fans should expect exciting performances from participating teams. “All is set for the tournament that is to begin Saturday morning. More than 20 teams have confirmed participation and we expect entertaining moments for our fans,” Moseti said. He assured fans and teams that adequate security measures had been put in place to ensure a safe and enjoyable tournament. The competition has received a major financial boost, with SportPesa increasing its sponsorship of the National Sevens Circuit from Sh16 million to Sh34 million, while Tusker has contributed Sh1.5 million towards the tournament. Moseti said the teams are highly motivated and predicted a competitive championship, adding that fans could witness a new winner emerge. Hosts Nakuru RFC, popularly known as Wanyore, received a further boost after Smart Application unveiled a Sh3 million sponsorship package to support the team’s preparations. The sponsorship is expected to strengthen Nakuru RFC’s role as a leading rugby development platform in the county and a pathway for players seeking opportunities at national level. Moseti explained that Division One will maintain its traditional format, with 16 teams divided into four pools of four. After the opening day’s pool matches, the top two teams from each pool will advance to the Cup quarter-finals on day two before proceeding to the semi-finals and final. The remaining eight teams will compete in placement playoffs to determine positions nine to 16. Division Two, however, will undergo changes, with the number of participating teams reduced from 20 to 16. The teams will now be divided into four pools of four, adopting a similar structure to Division One, where teams progress from pool matches to quarter-finals, semi-finals and finals. The Division Two lineup will include four teams relegated from Division One in the previous leg, the top four finishers from Division Two, excluding the promoted team, and nine other teams, with priority given to regional teams from host areas. In the women’s category, the eight participating teams will compete in a single division divided into two pools of four teams each. All teams will progress to the quarter-finals after pool matches, with the top performers advancing to the semi-finals and final. The other teams will compete in classification matches to determine their final rankings. The Division One pools for the main Cup competition feature some of Kenya’s top rugby clubs. Pool A consists of Kenya Harlequin, Zetech University, Menengai Oilers and Mombasa RFC. Pool B includes KCB Rugby, Nondescripts, Mwamba RFC and Nakuru RFC. Pool C brings together KU Blakblad, defending champions Strathmore Leos, MMUST and Catholic Monks. Pool D comprises Kabras Sugar, Daystar Falcons, Stallions Rugby and Kabarak University. The Prinsloo Sevens will open a six-leg 2026 National Sevens Circuit running from July 25 to September 13, featuring elite men’s and women’s rugby clubs across the country. Defending champions KCB Rugby enter the competition as favourites after a dominant 2025 campaign in which they accumulated 126 points and won four of the six tournament titles. However, they are expected to face stiff competition from Strathmore Leos, who defeated KCB at the Prinsloo and Embu legs last season, as well as other strong contenders including Kabras Sugar, Menengai Oilers and Kenya Harlequin. After Nakuru, teams will move to Kisumu for the Dala Sevens at Jomo Kenyatta Stadium from August 1 to 2, followed by Kabeberi Sevens at RFUEA Grounds in Nairobi on August 15 and 16. The circuit will continue with Driftwood Sevens at Mombasa Sports Club on August 22 and 23, Embu Sevens at Embu Stadium on September 5 and 6, before concluding with Christie Sevens at RFUEA Grounds in Nairobi on September 12 and 13. SportPesa representative Mercy Kabui said the company’s continued investment in rugby is aimed at supporting local talent and promoting home-grown sports. Kabui said the sponsorship reflects the company’s commitment to grassroots development and providing opportunities for young athletes to grow their skills. “Rugby is one of the sports that Kenyans hold dear to their hearts and we are pleased to renew the Sevens Circuit sponsorship for the next two years,” she said. Events Coordinator Kevin Odhiambo said the National Sevens Circuit has become an important platform for showcasing Kenya’s rugby talent and bringing fans together across the country. He noted that many emerging players who participate in the circuit eventually progress to represent Kenya on international platforms. By Jane Ngugi and Dennis Rasto
